Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Compare exact text, normalized text, and a list of approved names. Explain what each check preserves.
  • Use a regular expression to check a number’s boundaries, then explain why finding the number still leaves the claim unverified.
  • Read a fee amount from a known format, convert it to a number, and compare it with the approved fee.
  • Write a table of expected judgments for punctuation, negation, a wrong amount, and a valid paraphrase.
  • Calculate precision and recall for a small set of reviewed replies and report which cases still need review.

Why This Lesson Matters

A customer with ₹4,999 in Harbor Leaf Bank’s Standard Savings account asks what fee applies on July 15, 2026. The bank’s approved policy, SV-2 §2, says the minimum is ₹5,000 and the fee is ₹100 per month below that balance. The saved reply says “Monthly fee: ₹100.” A test that looks for the text “100” gives it a pass.

Now read “Monthly fee: ₹1000.” The same test still finds “100,” even though the fee is ten times too large. Make the rule stricter and another problem appears. A reply that says “You pay one hundred rupees each month” may fail an exact text check even though it communicates the approved fee.

You’ll use the same question to find out where each rule helps and where it gets in the way. The bank, policy, replies, and judgments below are fictional. Allow about 4.5 hours, including time to predict the experiments and complete the assignment.

Beginner Explanation

1. Start with text you can compare

Suppose the bank asks for the fee in a fixed format so another program can read it. If the expected text is “Monthly fee: ₹100.” and the actual text is the same, a character-by-character check passes. That’s an exact match. A missing period or an extra space would make it fail. The check is deterministic, meaning the same text and rule give the same result each time.

An exact match makes sense if the period is part of the format the bank requires. If the customer simply wants a clear answer, both versions can convey the same fee. Decide which behaviour the check is measuring before treating a mismatch as a wrong answer.

2. Agree which differences can be ignored

A teammate types “ STANDARD SAVINGS ” in a field for the account name. It looks like the same account. You can trim the extra spaces at the ends, collapse repeated spaces inside, and make the comparison ignore capital letters. Applying agreed changes before comparing is normalization.

Do this only where the change preserves the information you need. For an account-name field, repeated spaces may be harmless. For a money field, removing every mark can change the value. “₹1.00” and “₹100” become the same text if you blindly delete the period.

Computers use a standard called Unicode to represent text characters. For example, the full-width letter “Ｓ” takes up more space on the page and has a different stored representation from “S.” Python’s Unicode normalization form called NFKC can turn that full-width letter into the ordinary one. It can also fold other characters, such as turning “²” into “2.” Apply it only when your field’s rules permit those changes. In the lab, you’ll try it on the account name. The fee reader uses its own separate format.

The bank may also accept “Standard Savings Account” as a name for the same product. An alias is another approved name for the same thing. Pick one canonical name, meaning the name you store as the standard, and map reviewed aliases to it. If a name is unfamiliar, leave it for review. A similar-looking product could carry different fees.

3. Find complete numbers, then read the claim

A substring is a piece of text that appears inside a larger string. “100” is a substring of “1000.” It also appears in “The fee is ₹80, not ₹100.” The substring check answers whether some characters occur. The fee question asks what the reply actually says the customer must pay.

A regular expression, or regex, describes a text pattern. A boundary in that pattern can help you find “100” as a separate number in the examples above. It keeps “100” inside “1000” from matching. The separate number still matches in “not ₹100.” A boundary test tells you where the number occurs, while the neighbouring words tell you what the reply claims.

If the bank asks for exactly one field such as “Monthly fee: ₹100.”, check the full format and read the digits as a Python integer, a whole number. Compare the resulting number with the approved 100 rupees. This is a typed check because it compares numbers after reading the text. The word “Monthly” in the agreed format establishes the time period. The pattern in this lesson accepts only whole, nonnegative rupee amounts in that format, with an optional final period. Natural customer replies outside the format still need a reviewer.

4. Test your checker with replies someone has already reviewed

Write a row for each saved reply before running a rule. Include the policy, the reply, and whether a reviewer says the reply gives the right monthly fee. Then add the rule’s result. A table like this is a truth table for your checks. It shows where the rule agrees with your expected judgments and where it gets them wrong.

Suppose a rule marks four replies correct and a reviewer agrees on two of them. Its precision is two out of four, or 50%. Precision asks how many of the rule’s passes were deserved. If the reviewer found three correct replies in all, the rule’s recall is two out of three, or about 66.7%. Recall asks how many of the correct replies the rule found.

The passes a reviewer agrees with are true positives. A wrong reply that the rule passes is a false positive, or false pass. A correct reply the rule rejects is a false negative, or false failure. If a conservative rule sends a correct reply to review, it has yet to find that pass automatically. Report pending reviews separately. If a request never returned a reply, mark it UNSCORABLE. There’s no text to check, and it should stay visible as an execution outcome.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Decide whether a difference matters

User question. “Which savings account does this fee apply to?” The app expects an account name.

Approved reference. The policy names Standard Savings. The bank also approves “Standard Savings Account” as another name for it.

Actual LLM response. The saved field reads “ STANDARD SAVINGS ”.

Assessment. A character-by-character comparison fails. Trim the outside spaces, collapse the gaps, and compare without case. Now both names match. If the field instead reads “Standard Savings Account,” spacing rules alone leave an extra word. Look up the approved alias and store “Standard Savings.” This verifies the account name under the bank’s rules. It gives you no evidence that the rest of a reply states the fee correctly.

Failure classification. Treat the original exact-match failure as a false failure if the field allows these variations. Keep a counterexample such as “Premium Savings” so a rule cannot pass every name that contains “Savings.”

Example 2. Check what the number is doing

User question. “What monthly fee is due at ₹4,999 in Standard Savings on July 15?”

Approved reference. SV-2 §2 requires a ₹100 monthly fee at that balance. The lab’s fixed output format is “Monthly fee: ₹100.”, with the period optional.

Actual LLM response. One saved reply says “Monthly fee: ₹1000.” Another says “The fee is ₹80, not ₹100.”

Assessment. Both contain “100,” so a substring rule passes both. A number-boundary regex rules out the first and still matches the second. In the fixed format, read the first amount as the integer 1000. It fails the comparison with 100. The second reply needs review under the format check. A reviewer can then see that it asserts ₹80 and rejects the approved amount.

Failure classification. Both saved replies are incorrect. Count a false pass each time a rule accepts one. Keep the regex result as evidence of a text match, then use the fixed format or a reading of the whole claim to decide whether it found the right fee.

Example 3. Choose a rule for the job

User question. “At a balance of ₹4,999, what fee would I pay each month for Standard Savings on July 15?” The review sheet includes five saved replies and one request that timed out.

Approved reference. SV-2 §2 supports ₹100 per month. Reviewers accept equivalent wording about that amount and frequency.

Actual LLM response. A says “Monthly fee: ₹100.” B omits the period. C says “The fee is ₹80, not ₹100.” D says “Monthly fee: ₹1000.” E says “You pay one hundred rupees each month.” F returned no reply.

Assessment. A, B, and E give the correct fee. C and D give the wrong fee. A substring rule for “100” passes A through D, so two of its four passes are right. It finds two of the three correct replies. The typed check automatically passes A and B, fails D, and sends C and E to review. F stays unscorable under either rule.

Failure classification. The substring rule produces two false passes and one false failure. The typed rule has no false passes in these examples, but it still misses E as an automatic pass and needs two reviews. For a fixed output field, the typed check is a useful starting point. For natural replies, keep the review step. The small set demonstrates particular failure modes and supplies no estimate of live performance.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Every block is a complete Python 3.10+ program using only built-in features or the standard library. All replies and judgments are supplied as fictional practice data.

  1. Select Open Python Editor to open an editor in a separate tab. There is also an editor link next to every Python block.
  2. Select Copy Code, then paste the entire block into the editor yourself. Replace any text already there.
  3. Click Run. Open Expected output in the lesson and compare it with the editor’s output.
  4. Predict the experiment result, make the one specified edit, and click Run again. Compare with the second Expected output.

Keep the spaces at the start of lines. If you get an error while editing, paste the original block and check it before trying the edit again.

Step 1 — Check the exact text

Begin with the bank’s fixed fee format. Python will compare the expected string with one saved reply. A string is text between quotes. A name such as reply holds that text. Use = to store it and == to compare two values. The comparison produces True or False, and print() shows that result.

Copy the block, replace the editor contents, and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
expected = "Monthly fee: ₹100."
reply = "Monthly fee: ₹100."

print("Exact match:", reply == expected)
Expected output
Exact match: True

The two strings contain the same characters. Python can make that comparison without reading the bank policy.

Experiment. Remove only the final period from reply. Run again.

Expected output
Exact match: False

The last character is now different, so the exact match fails. The amount and frequency stayed the same.

Checkpoint. Would you mark the edited customer answer factually wrong? The policy fact is unchanged. Decide separately whether the format requires that period.

Step 2 — Ignore agreed differences in an account name

The same account name can arrive in capital letters or with repeated spaces. Use split() to split the name into pieces at whitespace, the spaces and similar gaps in text. In " ".join(words), the quoted space is the separator that goes between those pieces. casefold() prepares text for a comparison that ignores differences in letter case.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run. The function starts with def and takes one name each time you call it. return hands the cleaned name back.

Open Python Editor 
def normalize_name(name):
    words = name.split()
    return " ".join(words).casefold()


expected = "Standard Savings"
reply = "  STANDARD   SAVINGS  "

print("Exact match:", reply == expected)
print("Cleaned reply:", normalize_name(reply))
print("Normalized match:", normalize_name(reply) == normalize_name(expected))
Expected output
Exact match: False
Cleaned reply: standard savings
Normalized match: True

Splitting and rejoining removes the outside gaps and leaves one space inside. The cleaned versions use the same case.

Experiment. Change only reply to " PREMIUM SAVINGS " and run again.

Expected output
Exact match: False
Cleaned reply: premium savings
Normalized match: False

The same cleanup leaves the product name different, so the comparison still distinguishes these two accounts.

Checkpoint. Which changes did you decide to ignore? Spaces and letter case in the account field. This result says nothing about whether two differently named accounts share a policy.

Step 3 — Use a reviewed list of aliases

The bank accepts the text “Standard Savings Account” as an alias. A dictionary stores a name and its associated value in curly braces. aliases.get(key) retrieves the value for the supplied key and gives None when it cannot find one. Here None means the list contains no approved match.

The line from unicodedata import normalize makes Python’s standard Unicode helper available. Use NFKC on the account field before cleaning spaces and case. The if account is None condition handles a name the dictionary couldn’t find. The indented else block handles a name it found. Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
from unicodedata import normalize


def account_key(name):
    name = normalize("NFKC", name)
    return " ".join(name.split()).casefold()


aliases = {
    "standard savings": "Standard Savings",
    "standard savings account": "Standard Savings",
}
reply = "Ｓtandard Savings Account"
account = aliases.get(account_key(reply))

if account is None:
    print("Review: account name not recognized")
else:
    print("Canonical account:", account)
Expected output
Canonical account: Standard Savings

NFKC changes the full-width “Ｓ” to “S.” Cleanup turns the name into a dictionary key that already exists, so the program prints the canonical name saved under that key.

Experiment. Change only reply to "Standard-Savings Account" and run again.

Expected output
Review: account name not recognized

The hyphen stays in the cleaned key. This dictionary gives no match, so review the name before adding it as a new alias.

Checkpoint. Can you apply the same cleanup to every field? Use it only where the transformations preserve what the field is supposed to mean. For this check, the bank reviewed two account names.

Step 4 — Check the number’s boundaries

A substring search with in finds literal text wherever it appears. Import Python’s standard re module to try a pattern instead. In r"\b100\b", r tells Python to keep the backslashes for the regex, and \b means a boundary between a word character and a non-word character or the start or end of text. Digits are word characters, so there is no boundary between “100” and the last “0” in “1000.” re.search() returns None if it finds no match. is not None checks for a match.

Copy the complete block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
import re

reply = "Monthly fee: ₹1000."

print("Substring found:", "100" in reply)
print("Number pattern found:", re.search(r"\b100\b", reply) is not None)
Expected output
Substring found: True
Number pattern found: False

The substring occurs inside 1000. The pattern requires the boundary after 100, so it rejects this occurrence.

Experiment. Set only reply to "The fee is ₹80, not ₹100." and run again.

Expected output
Substring found: True
Number pattern found: True

Now the number is separate, and the pattern matches. The word “not” tells you that the reply denies this amount.

Checkpoint. Did the pattern verify the monthly fee? It found “100” with a boundary on each side. To check which amount the reply asserts, read the words around it. This pattern can also find “100” inside “100.50” because the decimal point marks a boundary.

Step 5 — Read a whole-rupee fee from a fixed format

Ask Python to match the entire field. re.fullmatch() requires a match from start to finish. In the pattern below, [0-9]+ means one or more digits from 0 through 9. Parentheses keep those digits as a group you can read back. [.]? makes a literal final period optional. match.group(1) reads the first group, and int() changes that string of digits into a whole number. strip() trims whitespace from the outside of the field.

Copy the block and click Run. Compare the displayed amount with the approved fee.

Open Python Editor 
import re

expected_rupees = 100
reply = "Monthly fee: ₹1000"

match = re.fullmatch(r"Monthly fee: ₹([0-9]+)[.]?", reply.strip())
if match is None:
    print("Review: could not read the fee field")
else:
    actual_rupees = int(match.group(1))
    print("Read rupees:", actual_rupees)
    print("Fee matches:", actual_rupees == expected_rupees)
Expected output
Read rupees: 1000
Fee matches: False

The full field matches the format, so Python compares 1000 and 100 as numbers.

Experiment. Change only reply to "Monthly fee: ₹100" and run again.

Expected output
Read rupees: 100
Fee matches: True

The pattern accepts the field without a period and the amounts now agree. Step 1’s literal check would reject the missing period.

Checkpoint. What if the reply says “You pay one hundred rupees each month”? This pattern would ask for review. The typed check measures the agreed field, so a reviewer must judge replies outside it.

Step 6 — Measure the substring rule against reviewed replies

Use the five replies from Example 3 that arrived. A reviewer has already judged each one. Put the replies and their expected judgments into pairs, then use for reply, correct in reviewed: to give the two values in each pair names. predicted holds what the substring rule says. Each pair is written in parentheses. The and test requires both conditions. elif tries the next condition when the one above didn’t run.

Copy the block and click Run. Divide the correct automatic passes by all automatic passes for precision. Divide the same correct automatic passes by all replies the reviewer accepted for recall. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. round(value, 1) gives one decimal place. Both denominators are positive in this lesson.

Open Python Editor 
reviewed = [
    ("Monthly fee: ₹100.", True),
    ("Monthly fee: ₹100", True),
    ("The fee is ₹80, not ₹100.", False),
    ("Monthly fee: ₹1000.", False),
    ("You pay one hundred rupees each month.", True),
]

true_passes = 0
false_passes = 0
missed_passes = 0
needle = "100"

for reply, correct in reviewed:
    predicted = needle in reply
    if predicted and correct:
        true_passes = true_passes + 1
    elif predicted:
        false_passes = false_passes + 1
    elif correct:
        missed_passes = missed_passes + 1

print("True passes:", true_passes)
print("False passes:", false_passes)
print("Missed passes:", missed_passes)
print("Precision (%):", round(100 * true_passes / (true_passes + false_passes), 1))
print("Recall (%):", round(100 * true_passes / (true_passes + missed_passes), 1))
Expected output
True passes: 2
False passes: 2
Missed passes: 1
Precision (%): 50.0
Recall (%): 66.7

Two of four automatic passes are correct. Two of the three reviewed correct replies got an automatic pass.

Experiment. Change only needle = "100" to needle = "100." and run again.

Expected output
True passes: 1
False passes: 1
Missed passes: 2
Precision (%): 50.0
Recall (%): 33.3

Requiring a period drops the wrong 1000 claim and also drops the valid reply without a period. The negated amount still ends in “100.” Precision stays at one half and recall drops.

Checkpoint. Did tightening the search make it a better checker? It removed one false pass and lost one valid pass. The reviewed replies tell you which errors changed. This small set gives no general performance rate.

Step 7 — Compare the rules and retain cases for review

Put both rules beside the same reviewed judgments. Run the format check in a function and return a result for each reply. None stands for a timeout with no saved text. The first condition returns UNSCORABLE before the code tries to read the text. An unfamiliar format returns REVIEW. A readable field returns PASS or FAIL according to its amount.

Copy the full block and click Run. The loop unpacks each case’s ID, reply, and reviewer judgment, then prints the two rule outcomes beside that judgment. expected is a policy value, while human holds the result of a review already performed for the example.

Open Python Editor 
import re


def typed_fee(reply, expected):
    if reply is None:
        return "UNSCORABLE"
    match = re.fullmatch(r"Monthly fee: ₹([0-9]+)[.]?", reply.strip())
    if match is None:
        return "REVIEW"
    if int(match.group(1)) == expected:
        return "PASS"
    return "FAIL"


expected = 100
cases = [
    ("A", "Monthly fee: ₹100.", "PASS"),
    ("B", "Monthly fee: ₹100", "PASS"),
    ("C", "The fee is ₹80, not ₹100.", "FAIL"),
    ("D", "Monthly fee: ₹1000.", "FAIL"),
    ("E", "You pay one hundred rupees each month.", "PASS"),
    ("F", None, "UNSCORABLE"),
]

print("Case | Human | Substring | Typed")
for case_id, reply, human in cases:
    if reply is None:
        substring = "UNSCORABLE"
    elif "100" in reply:
        substring = "PASS"
    else:
        substring = "FAIL"
    print(case_id, "|", human, "|", substring, "|", typed_fee(reply, expected))
Expected output
Case | Human | Substring | Typed
A | PASS | PASS | PASS
B | PASS | PASS | PASS
C | FAIL | PASS | REVIEW
D | FAIL | PASS | FAIL
E | PASS | FAIL | REVIEW
F | UNSCORABLE | UNSCORABLE | UNSCORABLE

The typed check makes three automatic decisions about written replies, all in agreement with the reviewer. It leaves two to review and records one execution outcome.

Experiment. In row D only, change "Monthly fee: ₹1000." to "A ₹100 fee applies every day.". Keep its human label as FAIL because the frequency is wrong. Run again.

Expected output
Case | Human | Substring | Typed
A | PASS | PASS | PASS
B | PASS | PASS | PASS
C | FAIL | PASS | REVIEW
D | FAIL | PASS | REVIEW
E | PASS | FAIL | REVIEW
F | UNSCORABLE | UNSCORABLE | UNSCORABLE

The substring rule still finds 100. The typed check now sees an unfamiliar format and asks for review. The human label stays FAIL because the bank charges monthly.

Checkpoint. Does the typed rule understand daily and monthly fees? It recognizes the word “Monthly” in one format. Keep the reviewer’s result and the rule’s result side by side when you decide how much to automate.

## Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Decide what a mismatch means

The bank expects the field “Monthly fee: ₹100.” The reply omits the period. Give a judgment for a strict field that requires the period, then give a judgment for factual correctness. Write one formatting change you would allow for an account name and one you would avoid for a fee.

Practice 2. Write the expected judgments before running a rule

Use the approved ₹100 per month fee. Make a truth table for B, C, D, and E from Example 3. Write the human verdict first. Then predict the verdicts of an exact match against A and a substring check for “100.” Identify where the two rules make different mistakes.

Practice 3. Separate a match from a verified amount

In the fixed field, try “Monthly fee: ₹1000.” and “The fee is ₹80, not ₹100.” Which text would match the boundary pattern from Step 4? Which would the typed check fail, and which would it send to review? Use the policy to give a final human judgment for each.

Practice 4. Read a checker report

A reviewer accepts three replies out of five. A rule passes four, including two that the reviewer accepts. Calculate precision and recall. Then imagine you improve precision by sending two false passes to review and leave the other rows unchanged. Give the new automatic precision, recall, and review count. What should the team check before choosing the new rule?

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The missing period fails the strict format. It still states the approved amount and frequency. For an account field, collapsing repeated spaces can preserve the account name. For money, keep decimal separators unless the format tells you how to interpret them. Removing the period in “₹1.00” would turn one rupee into a string that looks like one hundred.

Solution 2

Use three columns in each row for human judgment, exact match, and substring match.

  • B, no period. PASS, FAIL, PASS. The exact match falsely fails it.
  • C, negates ₹100. FAIL, FAIL, PASS. The substring rule falsely passes it.
  • D, claims ₹1000. FAIL, FAIL, PASS. The substring rule falsely passes it.
  • E, amount in words. PASS, FAIL, FAIL. Both rules falsely fail it.

The strict rule rejects two valid alternatives in these four rows. The loose rule accepts the punctuation variant and misses why the two wrong claims contain the expected characters.

Solution 3

The boundary pattern misses 100 inside 1000 but finds the separate 100 after “not.” The typed check reads the first reply as 1000 and fails it. The second reply does not fit the agreed field format, so it goes to review. Both replies give the wrong fee. The reviewer reads the whole second statement and finds that it asserts ₹80.

Solution 4

Precision is two correct automatic passes divided by four automatic passes, or 50%. Recall is two correct automatic passes divided by all three reviewed correct replies, or about 66.7%. After the change, both automatic passes are correct, so precision is 100% on this sample. Recall stays at about 66.7%, and two cases now need review. Before choosing the new rule, check what happens to more examples, whether the team can handle reviews, and whether an important error could still pass.

Knowledge Check

  1. The two amounts are “₹1.00” and “₹100.” What mistake could a normalization rule make here?
  2. Your checker sees the full-width “Ｓ” in an account name. When would you fold it into ordinary “S”?
  3. An unfamiliar product name contains “Savings.” What would you do before treating it as a known alias?
  4. A boundary regex finds “100” in “not ₹100.” What can you conclude?
  5. The typed field expects a monthly fee but the saved reply says “₹100 per day.” Is a matching number enough for a pass?
  6. A new rule passes fewer replies and makes no false passes on this sample. What two counts should you check before calling it an improvement?
  7. A request timed out. Should it enter the table as a reply that failed the fee rule?
  8. You want to compare two checkers. Your teammate also replaced the reviewed judgments between runs. What would you do before crediting the change to the checker?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Removing punctuation can turn both amounts into the same text. Interpret punctuation using the field’s money format before comparing amounts.
  2. Do it if the account-name rules allow full-width and ordinary forms to stand for the same name. Check the resulting name against the approved list.
  3. Send it to review and check the product catalogue. Sharing a word gives you no basis to apply another account’s policy.
  4. The characters occur at the pattern’s boundaries. The phrase denies that amount. You need the whole claim to judge it.
  5. No. The policy is monthly. Under the lab’s typed format, this reply needs review. A human would fail it for frequency.
  6. Check how many correct replies still get an automatic pass and how many rows now need review. Precision alone can hide missed correct answers or a growing review queue.
  7. Record it as UNSCORABLE because there was no reply to read. Track it as an execution failure separately.
  8. Use one reviewed set with the same expectations for both checkers, then rerun them. A changed judgment can change a score without any change in either rule.

Independent Assignment

You’re reviewing a bank change that allows a second fixed label, “Fee per month.” The approved amount stays ₹100. Your job is to see which additional cases the updated rule can decide without reading every reply by hand.

  1. Copy the original Step 7 program into the editor. Add these two rows after F, before the closing square bracket in cases. Put a comma after each row. Keep all the earlier rows and human judgments unchanged.
  2. - Row G has reply "Fee per month: ₹100." and human judgment "PASS".
  3. - Row H has reply "Fee per day: ₹100." and human judgment "FAIL".
  4. Run the program. Record the two rules’ verdicts on G and H, what happened to the original rows, and how many typed reviews you now have.
  5. In the regex pattern only, replace Monthly fee with (?:Monthly fee|Fee per month). The vertical bar offers two labels. The ?: tells Python to group the choices without saving a group, so match.group(1) still reads the digits. Run again. Record the typed verdicts for G and H and the new review count.
  6. Write a recommendation. Say which format the rule now supports and why you’d still review some replies. Compare the rules on these same eight rows.
Check your assignment

With the original rule, G and H both get PASS from the substring rule and REVIEW from the typed rule. The earlier rows are unchanged. The typed rule now has four replies to review, C, E, G, and H. After extending the pattern, G gets an automatic PASS because its format and amount match. H still needs review because the daily format falls outside both allowed labels. The queue drops from four to three. F remains unscorable in both runs.

The revised rule can read both approved monthly labels. It automatically finds three of the four replies the reviewer accepted. It still can’t read the amount spelled out in E. Keep the wrong daily reply in the test sheet. This comparison shows one additional valid format on the supplied cases. It gives no estimate of how often future replies will arrive in a new format.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a substring as a fact. Check which amount the reply asserts, alongside its currency and frequency.
  • Cleaning every field the same way. Choose normalization for each field. Check a counterexample before ignoring a character.
  • Counting unresolved or absent replies as accepted. Report pending reviews and unscorable requests separately.
  • Reporting precision without coverage. Keep the number of correct replies the rule missed and the size of the review queue visible.
  • Changing the examples when changing the rule. Compare both rules on the same saved replies and reviewed judgments.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Start by deciding whether the field requires exact text or allows agreed variations. Check narrow formats with normalization, approved aliases, and typed comparisons where suitable. Use reviewed replies to measure where the rule passes the wrong answer or misses the right one. Keep a review path for claims the rule cannot read.

Beginner · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Read a saved fee reply as JSON and identify a broken record or a record with the wrong overall shape.
  • Check required fields, distinguish a missing value from an explicit null, and test allowed choices, types, and ranges.
  • Check the format version first and verify that fields agree with one another.
  • Compare a usable reply with the approved fee policy and decide what to do with an invalid or unscorable result.
  • Build a small set of saved tests with known outcomes and run the same checks on every case.

Why This Lesson Matters

Imagine the same fee printed in two boxes on a bank form. One box says the customer owes a fee. The other says the amount is zero. The amounts may be legible and every box may be filled in, but the teller still needs to stop and find out which box is right.

A Harbor Leaf Bank app has a similar problem. It asks its assistant to return a record it can use to display a Standard Savings fee. For a customer with ₹4,999, the approved monthly fee is ₹100. The app receives a record showing “fee due” with zero rupees. Before showing it to the customer, the app needs to check whether the record can be read, whether the fields make sense together, and whether the claim agrees with the policy.

The bank, policy, records, and judgments are fictional. Allow about 4.5 hours for the demonstrations, seven short Python activities, and independent practice.

Beginner Explanation

1. Start with the format a computer can read

Imagine you have to copy the fee from “You’ll pay one hundred rupees each month.” You can read that sentence, but a program would have to work out which words tell it the amount. Give the program a labelled box instead. In {"amount_rupees": 100}, the quotation marks mark the field name, the colon connects the name and value, and the braces enclose the record.

This text format is JSON. The app’s request for a predictable record is a request for structured output. When Python reads the JSON text and turns it into a value it can work with, it is parsing. For this example, the result is a dictionary, Python’s collection of named values. Leaving off the closing brace makes the text unreadable as JSON. That’s a parsing error.

Try putting square brackets around the whole record. In JSON, the brackets make an array, a list of values. Python can read that JSON as a list containing one dictionary. The fee screen expects just the dictionary, so it should check the overall shape before it tries to read a named field.

2. Agree on what belongs in the record

Suppose the app receives the status “needs review” and an amount of null. The reply explicitly says there’s no amount it can give. If the amount box is absent, the app can’t tell whether the assistant deliberately left it unknown or simply forgot the box.

Write the rules the app expects in one place. This agreement about a record’s shape, fields, and values is its schema. Checking a record against those rules is schema validation. The bank’s practice agreement uses three fields, all required.

  • Version. schema_version must be the whole number 1. Check the version before interpreting the other fields. A later format might store paise instead of rupees, so an unfamiliar version goes for review.
  • Status. status must be one of fee_due, no_fee, or needs_review. This closed set of choices is called an enum.
  • Amount. amount_rupees must be a whole number from 0 to 1000 inclusive, or null. That makes the field nullable even though its name is required. The range is a made-up limit for the app’s record format. It does not set the bank’s actual fee.

A value’s type tells the program what kind of value it is. 100 is a number, "100" is text, and true is a yes-or-no value called a boolean. A format that requires a whole number should catch the other two. In Python, JSON null becomes None, and JSON true becomes True. Use an exact integer type check in this lab because Python also treats booleans as a kind of integer in some checks.

3. Ask whether the fields agree

Put a valid status of fee_due next to a valid amount of 0. Each field satisfies its own rule, but together they contradict the definition of “fee due.” The app needs one more check.

When the status is fee_due, the amount must be greater than zero. When it is no_fee, the amount must be zero. When it is needs_review, the amount must be null. A rule that must hold across fields is a cross-field invariant. Try changing only the status from fee_due to no_fee while the amount is 0. The fields now agree. The app still needs the customer’s balance and the approved policy to decide whether zero is correct.

4. Check the claim against the evidence

Keep the record at version 1 with a positive amount of 80 and a status of fee_due. The agreed format can represent this claim. Now read the bank’s approved policy for the exercise, SV-2 §2 (section 2). On July 15, 2026, Standard Savings had a ₹5,000 minimum, and a ₹100 monthly fee applied below that minimum. At exactly ₹5,000, no below-minimum fee applied. With a verified balance of ₹4,999, the claim of ₹80 is wrong.

The last check compares the claim with a rule for the actual task. This is a business rule check. This lab supplies the applicable policy and the verified balance separately from the reply. A balance claimed by the assistant would be another piece of output to check.

When there’s a broken or inconsistent record, keep the failure reason and hold the reply back from the fee screen. A business mismatch also calls for review before showing a charge. A reply with missing policy evidence may be readable and usable in shape, but its claim still needs review. A timeout gives you no reply to check. Keep these outcomes separate so the team can tell which part of the app to investigate. The practice checker is scoped to saved records and the July policy it was given.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Read one fee record

User question. “What’s the monthly Standard Savings fee at ₹4,999 on July 15?” Check that the saved reply can be read as one fee record.

Approved reference. The app expects one JSON object. SV-2 §2 specifies a ₹100 monthly fee at that balance.

Actual LLM response. The saved text is {"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": 100.

Assessment. Find the opening brace and look for its closing partner. It’s missing. Parsing stops, so you can’t read any field from a reliable record. Add a closing brace to a copy. Python can now read it as a dictionary. Try enclosing the entire repaired record in square brackets. Python still reads the text, and the result is now a list.

Failure classification. Hold the original reply for a parsing error. Mark the array variant as the wrong shape. A successful parse only gets you to the point where you can start checking the fields.

Example 2. Compare a missing field with a null field

User question. “Can you confirm my fee?” The app hasn’t verified the balance. It wants a record that can represent that gap.

Approved reference. Version 1 requires the amount field on every reply. For needs_review, its value must be null.

Actual LLM response. The saved reply is {"schema_version": 1, "status": "needs_review"}.

Assessment. Read the record as JSON and confirm it’s one object. The status is allowed. Now check whether the amount field exists. It doesn’t, so the record fails the schema. Add "amount_rupees": null to a copy. The field is now present, and the status and value agree. Try changing null to 100. The number fits the range, but the pair is inconsistent.

Failure classification. Report a missing field in the original and a cross-field failure in the 100-rupee variant. The null version describes an unresolved case. Keep it in review until the balance and applicable policy can be verified.

Example 3. Compare a usable record with policy

User question. “What fee applies at a Standard Savings balance of ₹4,999 on July 15?” The app has independently verified the balance.

Approved reference. Version 1’s format permits the status fee_due and a positive whole-rupee amount up to 1000. SV-2 §2 requires ₹100 per month at this balance.

Actual LLM response. The assistant returns {"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": 80}.

Assessment. Parse the reply and check its shape and version. All fields are present. The status is allowed, 80 is in range, and the positive amount agrees with the status. Now compare the fee with the applicable policy. The balance is one rupee below the minimum, so the expected fee is ₹100. Change 80 to 100 in a copy. The first checks still pass, and the policy check now agrees.

Failure classification. Record the original as a business mismatch. Keep the policy excerpt and verified balance with the example. This test supports a verdict for this record on this date. It gives little evidence about how the assistant will handle another account or policy.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Each block is a complete program for Python 3.10 or newer. It comes with fictional replies and any policy data it needs. Use them as written when you first run the block.

  1. Select Open Python Editor to open a separate tab. The same editor link appears beside each block.
  2. Select Copy Code in the lesson, then paste the entire block into the editor yourself. Replace whatever is already there.
  3. Click Run. Open the first Expected output below the code and compare the lines.
  4. Predict the experiment result, make the stated edit, and run again. Then check the second Expected output.

Each activity starts from a fresh block. Keep the spaces at the start of lines. If an edit produces an error, paste the original and run it again before retrying the edit.

Step 1 — Read JSON text

Start with one record containing an amount. The amount is written inside a string, which is a piece of text. The outer single quotes tell Python where the JSON text starts and ends. The inner double quotes belong to the JSON field name. The = sign stores the text under the name raw.

import json makes Python’s built-in JSON tools available. json.loads(raw) reads the text stored in raw. Python tries the indented lines under try. If the JSON reader reports JSONDecodeError, the except block handles that specific error. Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
import json

raw = '{"amount_rupees": 100}'
try:
    record = json.loads(raw)
    print("Read:", record)
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    print("PARSE ERROR")
Expected output
Read: {'amount_rupees': 100}

The printed value uses Python’s dictionary display. Its single quotes show how Python displays the field name after reading it.

Experiment. Remove the closing } inside the text, keeping the outer quotes. Run again.

Expected output
PARSE ERROR

The incomplete JSON can’t be read. Python follows the error branch instead of printing a record.

Checkpoint. Does the original result verify ₹100? It verifies that the text can be read. You still need the customer’s applicable policy.

Step 2 — Check the overall shape before reading a field

An app that wants one dictionary should check the shape before asking for its amount. isinstance(record, dict) asks whether the value Python read is a dictionary. if runs its indented lines when that check succeeds. else handles the other outcome.

Copy the block and click Run. Both versions of this activity use deliberately readable JSON.

Open Python Editor 
import json

raw = '{"amount_rupees": 100}'
record = json.loads(raw)

if isinstance(record, dict):
    print("Shape: one record")
else:
    print("SHAPE ERROR: expected one object")
Expected output
Shape: one record

The braces gave Python a dictionary, so it takes the first branch.

Experiment. Replace the value of raw with '[{"amount_rupees": 100}]'. Run again.

Expected output
SHAPE ERROR: expected one object

The square brackets give Python a list, even with only one item. The shape check stops it before any field lookup.

Checkpoint. Did parsing fail in the experiment? Python successfully read a list. The app’s requirement for one object is what failed.

Step 3 — Distinguish null from a missing field

A reviewer needs to know whether the reply reported an unknown amount or omitted the field. "amount_rupees" not in record checks whether that field name is missing. record["amount_rupees"] reads the value only after the first condition rules out a missing field. elif means “otherwise, check this condition,” and is None checks for Python’s value representing JSON null.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
import json

raw = '{"status": "needs_review", "amount_rupees": null}'
record = json.loads(raw)

if "amount_rupees" not in record:
    print("SCHEMA ERROR: missing amount_rupees")
elif record["amount_rupees"] is None:
    print("Amount: present, unknown")
else:
    print("Amount:", record["amount_rupees"])
Expected output
Amount: present, unknown

The amount field exists. The value explicitly records that the amount is unknown.

Experiment. Change raw to '{"status": "needs_review"}' and run again.

Expected output
SCHEMA ERROR: missing amount_rupees

The first check finds that the key is absent. It reports the missing field before attempting to read a value.

Checkpoint. Why keep these outcomes separate? A null can be allowed by the format. A missing required field means the app never received the box it asked for.

Step 4 — Check the version, status, and amount

Check version 1 before interpreting its fields. type(amount) is int checks for a Python whole number, including zero but excluding booleans. and requires both checks to succeed, so Python tests the range only after it knows the value is an integer. 0 <= amount <= 1000 includes both endpoints. The parentheses around the three status strings keep them together as a group of allowed values.

Copy the block and click Run. These examples supply all three required fields so you can focus on the values.

Open Python Editor 
import json

raw = '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": "100"}'
record = json.loads(raw)
version = record["schema_version"]

if type(version) is int and version == 1:
    status = record["status"]
    amount = record["amount_rupees"]
    print("Status allowed:", status in ("fee_due", "no_fee", "needs_review"))
    print("Amount allowed:", amount is None or (type(amount) is int and 0 <= amount <= 1000))
else:
    print("SCHEMA ERROR: unsupported version")
Expected output
Status allowed: True
Amount allowed: False

The status is in the allowed group. The amount is text because the JSON quotes surround it. The or condition accepts null by itself. Otherwise it requires the amount to pass both numeric checks.

Experiment. Remove the quotes around the JSON value "100" in raw. Keep the quotes around the field name. Run again.

Expected output
Status allowed: True
Amount allowed: True

Python now reads an integer and checks that it’s in range. Its printed appearance alone wouldn’t tell you whether the original was a number.

Checkpoint. If the value were JSON true, would it pass? Python would read True. Its exact type is a boolean, so the numeric branch would reject it.

Step 5 — Check that the status and amount agree

The amount and status below have already passed the individual field checks. Test how they work together. One acceptable pair is fee_due with a positive amount. To compare an amount with zero safely here, check for None first. is not None means there is an amount, and the earlier field checks in this example establish that it is an integer.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
status = "fee_due"
amount = 0

fee_due = status == "fee_due" and amount is not None and amount > 0
no_fee = status == "no_fee" and amount == 0
needs_review = status == "needs_review" and amount is None

if fee_due or no_fee or needs_review:
    print("Fields agree")
else:
    print("SCHEMA ERROR: status and amount disagree")
Expected output
SCHEMA ERROR: status and amount disagree

The amount is allowed on its own, but zero doesn’t agree with fee_due. None of the three pairs matches.

Experiment. Change only status from "fee_due" to "no_fee". Run again.

Expected output
Fields agree

Now a recognized pair matches. The amount stays zero, and the check still needs an applicable policy and balance to decide whether zero is right for the customer.

Checkpoint. What amount could accompany needs_review? The rule expects None. Zero would claim an actual amount.

Step 6 — Compare the amounts with trusted evidence

Use two cases whose records passed the earlier checks. Compare an amount of 100 with what the bank charges at two different balances. Each item in cases holds three values written together in parentheses. for case_id, balance, amount in cases: gives a name to each value when the loop reaches that item. The nested if checks the balance. Its else sets the expected fee to zero at or above the threshold.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
cases = [
    ("A", 4999, 100),
    ("B", 5000, 100),
]

for case_id, balance, amount in cases:
    if balance < 5000:
        expected = 100
    else:
        expected = 0
    if amount == expected:
        result = "PASS"
    else:
        result = "BUSINESS MISMATCH"
    print(case_id, result, "| expected", expected, "| got", amount)
Expected output
A PASS | expected 100 | got 100
B BUSINESS MISMATCH | expected 0 | got 100

The two replies give the same amount. The verified balance makes the applicable fee different. In B, ₹5,000 is at the minimum, so the approved fee is zero.

Experiment. Change only the last value in B from 100 to 0. This step compares amounts after schema checks. In a complete record, the corrected zero amount would also require the no_fee status. Run again.

Expected output
A PASS | expected 100 | got 100
B PASS | expected 0 | got 0

Only B changes. Its amount now agrees with the policy. The result covers these two balances under the stated policy.

Checkpoint. Could you verify B’s verdict using only the assistant’s amount? You need the independently verified balance and the fee rule that applies on the given date.

Step 7 — Put each failure in the right place

Run all the checks in a function, a named block that Python can run for each case. def check_reply(raw, balance): gives names to two inputs. Each return ends the check for that case and hands the first outcome back to the reporting loop. Fixing that first problem may reveal another. The loop prints one outcome per case.

A balance of None means the trusted balance was unavailable. A raw reply of None means the request returned no text. Python treats them separately because one leaves an unresolved fact while the other leaves no reply to check. In the schema checks, != means “is different from.” Use not (...) to reverse the outcome of the condition inside the parentheses. This lab version checks required fields and ignores extra fields. Its JSON parser is used with the supplied examples. A stricter application may need to reject duplicate field names and nonstandard values such as NaN, which Python’s default reader can accept.

Copy the full block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
import json


def check_reply(raw, balance):
    if raw is None:
        return "UNSCORABLE: no reply"
    try:
        record = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return "PARSE ERROR"
    if not isinstance(record, dict):
        return "SHAPE ERROR: expected one object"

    if "schema_version" not in record:
        return "SCHEMA ERROR: missing schema_version"
    version = record["schema_version"]
    if type(version) is not int or version != 1:
        return "SCHEMA ERROR: unsupported version"
    for field in ("status", "amount_rupees"):
        if field not in record:
            return "SCHEMA ERROR: missing " + field

    status = record["status"]
    amount = record["amount_rupees"]
    if status not in ("fee_due", "no_fee", "needs_review"):
        return "SCHEMA ERROR: unknown status"
    if amount is not None and not (type(amount) is int and 0 <= amount <= 1000):
        return "SCHEMA ERROR: amount type or range"

    if status == "needs_review":
        if amount is not None:
            return "SCHEMA ERROR: status and amount disagree"
    elif (
        amount is None
        or (status == "fee_due" and amount == 0)
        or (status == "no_fee" and amount != 0)
    ):
        return "SCHEMA ERROR: status and amount disagree"

    if balance is None:
        return "REVIEW: no verified balance"
    if status == "needs_review":
        return "BUSINESS MISMATCH: expected a fee answer"

    if balance < 5000:
        expected = 100
    else:
        expected = 0
    if amount != expected:
        return "BUSINESS MISMATCH: wrong fee"
    return "PASS: agrees with July policy"


cases = [
    ("A", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": 100}', 4999),
    ("B", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "no_fee", "amount_rupees": 0}', 5000),
    ("C", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "needs_review"}', None),
    ("D", '{"amount_rupees": 100', 4999),
    ("E", '[]', 4999),
    ("F", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": true}', 4999),
    ("G", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": 0}', 4999),
    ("H", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "fee_due", "amount_rupees": 80}', 4999),
    ("I", '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "needs_review", "amount_rupees": null}', None),
    ("J", None, 4999),
]

for case_id, raw, balance in cases:
    print(case_id, check_reply(raw, balance))
Expected output
A PASS: agrees with July policy
B PASS: agrees with July policy
C SCHEMA ERROR: missing amount_rupees
D PARSE ERROR
E SHAPE ERROR: expected one object
F SCHEMA ERROR: amount type or range
G SCHEMA ERROR: status and amount disagree
H BUSINESS MISMATCH: wrong fee
I REVIEW: no verified balance
J UNSCORABLE: no reply

A and B agree with the policy on opposite sides of its fee rule. H passes the earlier checks and reaches a business mismatch. I can represent its unknown amount in the schema, so its next step is review. J never reaches parsing because it has no reply.

Experiment. In row H only, change schema_version from 1 to 2. Keep the amount at 80 and run again.

Expected output
A PASS: agrees with July policy
B PASS: agrees with July policy
C SCHEMA ERROR: missing amount_rupees
D PARSE ERROR
E SHAPE ERROR: expected one object
F SCHEMA ERROR: amount type or range
G SCHEMA ERROR: status and amount disagree
H SCHEMA ERROR: unsupported version
I REVIEW: no verified balance
J UNSCORABLE: no reply

H now stops at the version check. The checker needs a rule for version 2 before it can interpret its amount. The other rows are unchanged.

Checkpoint. Why keep the three outcomes in H, I, and J separate? H needs a compatible record or a supported version. I needs trusted evidence. J needs an investigation into why the app got no reply.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Separate broken text from the wrong shape

The app expects one object. Write a verdict for {"amount_rupees": 100 and for [{"amount_rupees": 100}]. Say which one Python can read and which one you would pass on to the field checks. Describe one change to each that would make its shape usable.

Practice 2. Check a whole number and an allowed status

In version 1, a reply contains "status": "charged" and "amount_rupees": true. Mark each field as allowed or disallowed and explain why. Then propose field values for a known 100-rupee fee. Explain what extra information you’d need to decide whether the corrected record tells the truth.

Practice 3. Separate the format from what it claims

Compare two complete version 1 replies for a verified July balance of ₹4,999. A says fee_due with 0. B says no_fee with 0. For each reply, decide whether its fields agree and whether you can show a charge based on that record. Use the policy to give the expected record.

Practice 4. Identify which evidence is missing

A version 1 reply says needs_review with a null amount. The customer asked about July 15, but the app cannot verify the balance. A colleague says the reply passes because null is allowed. What has been checked? What result should the fee evaluation record? Describe what the app could do next and how the conclusion would change with a verified balance of ₹5,000.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The first text is missing its closing brace, so parsing fails. Adding the brace gives you an object to inspect. Python can parse the second text, but it reads a list. Remove the surrounding brackets in a copy to get the single object. In both repaired examples, the object is ready for field checks. The version and status are still missing.

Solution 2

charged is outside the three allowed status values, and true becomes a boolean. Even though Python sometimes treats True like 1, the fee field requires the exact integer type. Use fee_due with the number 100 for a record that claims a known fee. To verify the claim, compare it with the applicable policy and a trusted balance.

Solution 3

A fails the cross-field rule because fee_due requires a positive amount. B passes the format because no_fee goes with zero. It fails the business check because ₹4,999 is below ₹5,000 and July’s policy charges ₹100 at that balance. Hold both original replies. The expected version 1 record says fee_due with the integer 100.

Solution 4

The version, fields, and combination of status and amount fit the schema. The team still lacks a trusted fact needed to verify a fee. Record REVIEW and obtain the verified balance through the app’s approved process. At ₹5,000 the July rule gives zero. Once that balance is known, the expected record is no_fee with 0. The unchanged needs_review reply then fails the expectation to answer a known case.

Knowledge Check

  1. A timeout gives you no text. A different request returns text with a missing brace. Which stage gets each record?
  2. A parser reads null successfully. Would you look up amount_rupees on the resulting value? Explain.
  3. A record arrives with version 2 and a field named amount_paise. Why pause before comparing it with a rupee amount?
  4. A reply says no_fee with a null amount. Both values are allowed individually. What should the checker do?
  5. Would a range check alone verify a fee of ₹80 at a July balance of ₹4,999? What evidence settles it?
  6. Why would accepting the string "100" by silently converting it hide something useful in a version 1 test?
  7. Two records for a verified balance of ₹5,000 each say no_fee with 0. One lacks a version. Why do their verdicts differ?
  8. The checker reports PASS on two known July cases. What claim can the team make, and what would it need to check before drawing the same conclusion about June?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Record the timeout as UNSCORABLE and keep the delivery failure visible. The second reply reaches the parser and gets a parsing error.
  2. No. JSON null becomes Python’s None, so the value is the wrong shape for named fields. Check the overall shape first.
  3. The version can change what a field means or how it’s measured. Find the approved rules for version 2 before interpreting or converting its amount.
  4. Report that the fields disagree. no_fee represents a known zero, so the pair requires the integer 0.
  5. The range admits 80. The verified balance and SV-2 show the approved amount is ₹100 because ₹4,999 is below the minimum.
  6. The assistant’s reply broke the requirement to supply a number. Silent conversion would hide that format issue from the test and could make different consumers behave differently.
  7. The app needs the version to know how to read each record. The one without a required version stops at the schema check. The complete one can reach the policy check and pass.
  8. Both supplied records agree with July’s policy for their verified balances. Before evaluating a June case, verify which version of the policy applied on the date in question and use a trusted balance for that case.

Independent Assignment

The bank has two more saved replies. One uses a new format the checker hasn’t been taught. The other reports uncertainty. Keep the original ten cases as a check on the behaviour that already works.

  1. Paste the full Step 7 block into the editor. Add K and L after J, before the closing square bracket of cases. Use the same three positions as the existing rows, with a comma after each row.
  2. - For K, use ID "K", the raw text '{"schema_version": 2, "status": "fee_due", "amount_paise": 10000}', and a verified balance of 4999.
  3. - For L, use ID "L", the raw text '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "needs_review", "amount_rupees": null}', and None for the balance.
  4. Run the program. Record the verdicts for both additions. Count how many of the original ten lines changed.
  5. The app verifies a balance of ₹5,000 for L. Change only L’s balance from None to 5000. Run again. Explain why the exact same raw reply now gets a different verdict.
  6. For L, replace the raw reply with a version 1 record that agrees with SV-2. Keep the verified balance and run a third time. Say how you would follow up on K and what the three runs demonstrate.
Check your assignment

K prints K SCHEMA ERROR: unsupported version in all three runs. This checker only has rules for version 1. Ask for the approved version 2 agreement and examples before interpreting the amount. Editing K’s version number alone would leave its format incompatible.

L first prints L REVIEW: no verified balance. After you supply 5000, it prints L BUSINESS MISMATCH: expected a fee answer. The schema still accepts the null with needs_review, but the trusted balance and policy now establish the expected fee.

In the third run, L’s raw text should be '{"schema_version": 1, "status": "no_fee", "amount_rupees": 0}'. It prints L PASS: agrees with July policy. The original ten lines remain the same across all three runs. The assignment shows what the app can conclude on these saved records. A compatible schema and a known policy answer still need to be checked separately in new cases.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading fields before checking the shape. A valid JSON list or null can still be unusable as a fee record.
  • Treating missing, null, and zero as interchangeable. Check whether the field exists, then check what the value means in the agreed format.
  • Checking fields in isolation. Test incompatible pairs as well as values outside the allowed choices or range.
  • Equating a valid form with a correct charge. Compare the claim with the policy and facts supplied independently.
  • Counting every error as a wrong fee. Report missing replies, parsing errors, schema problems, business mismatches, and unresolved evidence separately.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

First check that you received a reply you can parse. Check the record’s shape and version, then its fields and how they work together. Finally compare the claim with the evidence for that customer and date. Save a known example for each kind of failure so you can test future changes.
