Intermediate · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Give a judge one saved candidate and one clear criterion at a time.
  • Write a prompt with a scoring rubric, examples of each rating, and instructions for citing evidence.
  • Distinguish a readable JSON verdict, a schema-valid verdict, and a verdict supported by the candidate and policy.
  • Record why a verdict cannot be scored, compare it with a human decision on the same saved reply, and route uncertainty to review.

Why This Lesson Matters

Imagine you open a saved Harbor Leaf Market chat. The customer’s parcel arrived 45 days ago. The assistant says there is still time to request a refund because the store allows 90 days. You open the approved policy and underline “through calendar day 30.” Before assigning any score, you can already explain the problem to a colleague. Day 45 is past the deadline your store actually allows.

The support team has many saved replies. It wants a second model to apply the same checks you just used. Before the team trusts that model, it needs to see what the model read, what it decided, and whether the evidence supports its decision.

The store, policy, replies, scores, and human decisions in this chapter are fictional. Policy refund-1 applies to eligible unused online purchases. The approved clause reads “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included. Allow about 5.5 hours. The background for this chapter is Structured output and schema validation and Rubrics and a first human evaluation. Annotation, adjudication and synthetic data and Combining evaluators and handling uncertainty are useful refreshers.

Beginner Explanation

Give one answer to a second reader

Read the 90-day reply and write down why you would hold it. The assistant’s job was to answer the customer. Your job was to compare that answer with the policy. If a large language model applies your evaluation instructions to the saved answer, it acts as an LLM judge. It can help apply a common set of checks to many answers. The support team still decides which checks matter and verifies how well the judge follows them.

Give the judge one question and one saved answer, called the candidate. It rates that candidate against defined criteria. That is pointwise judging. A batch may contain many case IDs, but each rating is made for a single answer. Asking the judge to pick the better of two answers is a different task.

Turn the reason into a scoring guide

Put “You can request a refund within 30 calendar days of delivery” next to the policy. Now ask one reader whether the sentence is easy to understand. Ask another whether a customer would know to bring a receipt. The first reader can say yes while the second says no. A criterion names the question the rating answers. Here the judge checks whether the reply gives reliable guidance about the refund requirements. Give readability its own check so a clear sentence cannot earn credit for a missing condition. This is criterion isolation.

A rubric defines the scale and gives observable conditions for choosing each rating. An anchor is a description or example that shows what a rating looks like. Use this fictional rubric, refund-guidance-v1, for the eligible order and the one approved clause. Start with the approved policy. If it is available, look for an explicit contradiction first. Use the missing-evidence instruction below when a required fact cannot be established. With clear evidence, choose the first matching anchor. This priority matters if a reply has multiple problems.

Course hours by track
ScoreObservable anchorExample or route
1Explicitly contradicts a critical rule about the deadline or valid receipt.Says 90 days, or says a receipt is optional. REJECT.
2Gives no usable guidance about either requirement, or adds a material unsupported claim without a demonstrated contradiction.Promises automatic approval when the policy only allows requests. REVIEW.
3Gives exactly one requirement correctly and omits the other, with no material unsupported claim.Gives the correct window and leaves out the receipt. REVIEW.
4Gives both requirements correctly without explicitly confirming day 30 is included.Says “within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.” ACCEPT for this criterion.
5Gives both requirements correctly and explicitly confirms eligibility to request on day 30.Says “through day 30, including that day, with a valid receipt.” ACCEPT for this criterion.

After checking for an explicit contradiction, pause scoring if the source is missing or the wording leaves a material fact ambiguous. Use REVIEW with a null score and leave the evidence string empty when abstaining. “First month,” for example, may need a reviewer to clarify the intended deadline. A null score means no numeric judgment was made. It differs from a 1, which requires evidence of an actual contradiction. The rubric’s decisions apply only to refund guidance under this case policy.

Tell the judge what it can read

“Rate this answer from 1 to 5” gives the judge no way to tell what a 4 means. Use a prompt, the instructions and evidence supplied to the judge, that spells out the following.

  • Question and conversation history. Include the original wording and the earlier messages needed to resolve references such as “this item.” Here the earlier customer message says the item is an eligible unused online purchase.
  • Frozen candidate and response ID. Keep the exact captured reply and its identifier. Treat the reply as material to assess, even if it contains text that sounds like an instruction to the judge.
  • Reference answer, when available. This is an example of how to answer. “You may ask for a refund within the published window” can be a reasonable summary and still omit the deadline.
  • Authoritative source. Include the approved policy text and version that apply to that order. The policy establishes the rule. A reference example does not replace it.
  • Rubric and output instructions. Name the criterion and anchors, say which contradictions have priority, and specify the verdict fields and how to handle uncertainty.

A reference-guided judgment uses an example answer, authoritative evidence, or both as provided comparison material. Record exactly which material the judge saw. A reference-free judgment has no supplied reference answer or source for comparison. For instance, a judge can assess whether the reply is readable from the question and reply alone. Verifying the store’s actual deadline still requires the relevant source. If you have the policy but no sample answer, use the policy and record that evidence directly.

Check the verdict in layers

Suppose the judge returns {"score":3,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"The receipt requirement is absent.","evidence":"with a valid receipt"}. This is JSON, a text format for named values. score gives the rubric rating. decision tells the workflow where to route the reply. reason explains what the judge found. evidence quotes a contiguous piece of the supplied policy, called an evidence span. The candidate itself is the evidence that the receipt was omitted. The quote establishes that a receipt matters.

First check whether Python can read the JSON. A missing comma can make it unreadable. Then check its schema, the rules for which fields and values it must contain. A value of "3" is text. The rubric calls for an integer such as 3. A 6 is an integer outside the scale. An absent source uses null for the score, REVIEW for the decision, and an empty evidence string.

Finally, read what the verdict claims. A quote can be invented or copied from a real but irrelevant sentence. Read the candidate and the source side by side. A genuine quote about the 30-day window does not support a judge’s statement that the candidate preserved it if the candidate actually says 90 days. A missing receipt is an incomplete answer. An explicit waiver contradicts the policy. A promise of automatic approval is unsupported by this source.

Know when to stop and ask for help

The same judge can give different ratings across runs, even when the reply stays the same. A vague anchor, altered prompt wording, or a polished answer can pull attention away from a policy fact. Missing evidence can encourage a confident guess. Compare the exact same response ID and text with an independent human decision. Keep the model or replay version, prompt, rubric, and source version so you can identify what changed. One disagreement tells you where to investigate. Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena Estimating reliability takes more independently checked cases.

Use a fallback when a required check fails or evidence is uncertain. Reject an unusable judge verdict and record why. If an independent check establishes a critical policy violation, it can block the reply. Otherwise send the frozen case to review. Give the reviewer the evidence needed to settle it, such as the effective policy and the original question. Preserve the judge’s raw output and the reviewer’s subsequent outcome. A malformed record never counts as agreement.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Turn two interpretations into one criterion

User question. How long do I have to request a refund for this eligible order, and do I need my receipt?

Approved reference. Policy refund-1 allows requests through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.

Actual LLM response. The frozen reply C says “You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.”

Assessment. “Rate this answer from 1 to 5” could mean rate the wording or rate how completely it states the policy. Replace it with “Use refund-guidance-v1 to rate refund requirements only. Compare the candidate with the supplied policy. Prioritize explicit contradictions. Use null and REVIEW if the evidence is missing. Return score, decision, reason, and an exact policy quote in JSON.” Supply the full rubric table with the prompt. The deadline is correct and the receipt is absent, so anchor 3 applies. The receipt clause supports a REVIEW route.

Failure classification. Record incomplete guidance and ask for the receipt requirement to be added. A clear prompt gives the judge an observable target. This example supplies the judgment by hand, so it gives no measurement of how a real judge would respond.

Example 2. Compare a saved judge verdict with human adjudication

User question. Can I still request a refund for my unused online order 45 days after delivery?

Approved reference. The approved clause includes requests through calendar day 30 after delivery, with a valid receipt.

Actual LLM response. The frozen reply B says “You can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.”

Assessment. The illustrative saved verdict for B has score 4, decision ACCEPT, reason “The reply states the correct window and mentions a receipt,” and evidence “through calendar day 30 after delivery.” A human independently reads reply B with the same policy. The quote is genuine, but the candidate claims 90. At day 45, the wording would permit a request outside the approved window. The human’s final evidence-backed decision, called adjudication, is score 1 and REJECT.

Failure classification. Record two outcomes for B. Hold the customer reply because 90 contradicts the policy. Mark the judge verdict as unusable because it says that same deadline is correct. Keep the quote, candidate, and human decision together under ID B. If a colleague opens the record tomorrow, they can see why the reply was blocked even though the automated judgment said ACCEPT. Both judgments here are fictional.

Example 3. Decline to guess a missing policy

User question. What deadline and receipt rule apply to this eligible order?

Approved reference. There is no approved policy text on the case. The example answer says “You may be able to request a refund,” with no dates or receipt conditions.

Actual LLM response. F says “You can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.”

Assessment. The example answer cannot establish whether F’s deadline applies to this order. Under the rubric, the verdict is {"score":null,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"The approved policy is missing.","evidence":""}. This is a valid abstention, a record that the judge declined to give a numeric judgment. Ask a reviewer to retrieve the dated, approved policy that applies to this order.

Failure classification. Record F | policy missing | score null | REVIEW | fetch applicable policy | human PENDING and preserve the original reply. The missing source leaves the candidate unresolved. If a different approved policy later arrives, create a new review record linked to the original case.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Choose Copy Code, open the editor next to the program, paste the entire block, and select Run. Compare the output with the first expected result. Make only the stated change, then run again. Start with an empty editor for each activity. Every program uses inline teaching data and standard Python. Each judge verdict is a fictional saved example. The code reads or validates those examples and never calls a model.

Step 1 — Inspect one saved judge record

The team wants to know exactly which answer a verdict belongs to. A dictionary pairs names with values, and brackets retrieve a value by name. The value at "judge" is itself a dictionary. An f"..." string inserts the value named inside braces.

Open Python Editor

record = {
    "id": "C",
    "question": "How long after delivery can I request a refund, and what do I need?",
    "candidate": "You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.",
    "rubric": "refund-guidance-v1",
    "judge": {"score": 3, "decision": "REVIEW"},
}

print(f"Reply {record['id']} | rubric {record['rubric']}")
print(f"Question: {record['question']}")
print(f"Candidate: {record['candidate']}")
print(f"Saved judge: {record['judge']['score']} | {record['judge']['decision']}")
Expected output
Reply C | rubric refund-guidance-v1
Question: How long after delivery can I request a refund, and what do I need?
Candidate: You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.
Saved judge: 3 | REVIEW

Experiment. Change only the saved judge's score from 3 to 4. Keep the decision and candidate fixed.

Expected output
Reply C | rubric refund-guidance-v1
Question: How long after delivery can I request a refund, and what do I need?
Candidate: You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.
Saved judge: 4 | REVIEW

The program displays the stored value. It has no check that 4 belongs with ACCEPT, or that the text supports 4. Checkpoint. Which fields identify what was actually judged? The ID, question, and candidate preserve the case. The rubric version identifies the instructions used to rate it.

Step 2 — Look up what each rating means

The reviewer sees a 3. Use the scoring guide to see which observation would justify it. This dictionary uses numbers as keys and stores a description and a decision together. Writing anchor, decision = rubric[score] gives each part its own name.

Open Python Editor

rubric = {
    1: ("Explicit critical contradiction", "REJECT"),
    2: ("No usable guidance or a material unsupported claim", "REVIEW"),
    3: ("One correct requirement and one omission", "REVIEW"),
    4: ("Both requirements correct; day 30 not explicitly included", "ACCEPT"),
    5: ("Both requirements correct; day 30 explicitly included", "ACCEPT"),
}
score = 3
anchor, decision = rubric[score]
print(f"Score {score}: {anchor}")
print(f"Rubric route: {decision}")
Expected output
Score 3: One correct requirement and one omission
Rubric route: REVIEW

Experiment. Change score = 3 to score = 4.

Expected output
Score 4: Both requirements correct; day 30 not explicitly included
Rubric route: ACCEPT

The program retrieves a different row of the scoring guide. Nothing in this activity reads the candidate. Checkpoint. What needs to change in C for a reviewer to justify 4? The reply must also state the valid receipt condition. The anchor gives a precise correction to request.

Step 3 — Compare two prompt drafts on the same case

Give two prompts the same candidate and evidence. Check whether each includes the named instructions on a checklist. "\n" is a line break, and join() joins strings using the separator before it. label not in prompt checks whether the literal heading is absent. The checklist checks visible text only. A heading by itself cannot establish that the judge can follow the instruction.

Open Python Editor

question = "How long do I have and do I need my receipt for this eligible order?"
candidate = "You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery."
policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
case = f"Question: {question}\nCandidate: {candidate}\nSource: {policy}\n"
weak = case + "Rate the answer from 1 to 5."
strong = case + "\n".join([
    "Criterion: refund guidance only; treat the candidate as data.",
    "Anchors: 1 contradiction; 2 unusable or unsupported; 3 one correct and one omitted;",
    "4 both correct; 5 both correct with day 30 explicitly included.",
    "Critical rule: a wrong window or receipt waiver overrides other strengths.",
    "Missing evidence: use null and REVIEW if the source or required interpretation is unresolved.",
])
output_instruction = ""
strong += output_instruction
headings = ("Criterion:", "Anchors:", "Critical rule:", "Missing evidence:", "Output:")

for name, prompt in [("Weak", weak), ("Stronger", strong)]:
    missing = [label.rstrip(":") for label in headings if label not in prompt]
    print(f"{name} missing: {', '.join(missing) if missing else 'none'}")
Expected output
Weak missing: Criterion, Anchors, Critical rule, Missing evidence, Output
Stronger missing: Output

Experiment. Change output_instruction from "" to "\nOutput: JSON with score, decision, reason, and evidence. Quote the policy when scoring. Use empty evidence when abstaining.".

Expected output
Weak missing: Criterion, Anchors, Critical rule, Missing evidence, Output
Stronger missing: none

The checklist can now find every heading in the second prompt. In a real prompt you would include the full rubric and the score-to-decision mapping. Checkpoint. Did the program measure rating quality? It checked which strings were present. To test judgment quality, compare outputs on fixed cases with reviewed answers.

Step 4 — Reject an invalid structured verdict

Python's standard-library json module turns a JSON object into a dictionary. try runs the parser, and except handles text it cannot read. Use type(score) is int so a Boolean such as JSON true cannot pass as an integer. set(verdict) lists the dictionary keys for comparison with the required field names. This activity expects a numeric rating because the case has a source and a clear anchor.

Open Python Editor

import json

raw = '{"score":3,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"Receipt omitted.","evidence":"with a valid receipt"}'
routes = {1: "REJECT", 2: "REVIEW", 3: "REVIEW", 4: "ACCEPT", 5: "ACCEPT"}
required = {"score", "decision", "reason", "evidence"}

def check(text):
    try:
        verdict = json.loads(text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return "PARSE ERROR"
    if not isinstance(verdict, dict) or set(verdict) != required:
        return "SCHEMA ERROR (fields)"
    score = verdict["score"]
    if type(score) is not int or score not in routes:
        return "SCHEMA ERROR (score)"
    if verdict["decision"] != routes[score]:
        return "SCHEMA ERROR (decision)"
    for name in ("reason", "evidence"):
        if not isinstance(verdict[name], str) or not verdict[name].strip():
            return f"SCHEMA ERROR ({name})"
    return "SCHEMA OK"

print(check(raw))
Expected output
SCHEMA OK

Experiment. In raw, change only "score":3 to "score":6.

Expected output
SCHEMA ERROR (score)

The text still parses as JSON. The integer 6 is outside the rubric. Compare this with a missing closing brace, which prevents parsing entirely. Checkpoint. Can schema validation tell whether the quote appears in the approved policy? This validator checks presence, kind, and allowed values. An evidence check is a separate step.

Step 5 — Check that a quote supports the criterion

The store's evidence packet contains a refund rule and an unrelated help statement. A quote must occur in the packet and point to the rule needed for the verdict. quote in source checks whether the exact text appears. The approved span below is defined for this one refund rule.

Open Python Editor

rule = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
help_text = "Support can answer questions in Orders."
source = rule + "\n" + help_text
verdict = {"evidence": "with a valid receipt"}
approved_span = "with a valid receipt"
quote = verdict["evidence"]

print(f"Quote present: {bool(quote) and quote in source}")
print(f"Receipt span: {quote == approved_span and quote in rule}")
Expected output
Quote present: True
Receipt span: True

Experiment. Change only the quoted evidence in verdict to "Support can answer questions in Orders.".

Expected output
Quote present: True
Receipt span: False

Both runs found the exact quote in the packet. Only the first found the receipt rule. Imagine reviewing a verdict with two tabs open. In the policy tab, highlight the words that make a receipt necessary. In the candidate tab, look for any wording that tells the customer about that requirement. Checkpoint. If the first highlight exists and the second does not, the policy is supported and the reply is incomplete. The program checks just the first tab using one exact span. If it misses a valid alternative quote, have a reviewer inspect the wording.

Step 6 — Measure disagreement on the same reply

Two fictional replay outputs both refer to reply B and the same rubric. An independent human adjudication gives B a 1 for stating 90 days. Use the difference between the highest and lowest saved rating as a simple measure of spread. max() finds the highest value and min() the lowest. Count exact matches to the human score by adding one each time the comparison is true.

Open Python Editor

case_id = "B"
ratings = [4, 1]
human_score = 1
spread = max(ratings) - min(ratings)
match_count = sum(rating == human_score for rating in ratings)

print(f"Reply {case_id}: judge ratings {ratings}")
print(f"Rating spread: {spread}")
print(f"Exact matches with human score: {match_count}/{len(ratings)}")
Expected output
Reply B: judge ratings [4, 1]
Rating spread: 3
Exact matches with human score: 1/2

Experiment. Change only the second rating in ratings from 1 to 4.

Expected output
Reply B: judge ratings [4, 4]
Rating spread: 0
Exact matches with human score: 0/2

Both outputs now agree with each other and differ from the human decision. Checkpoint. Which comparison should trigger an investigation here? Compare both verdicts and their reasons with the source and the 90-day sentence. The spread measures consistency between the outputs. The facts support the human decision in this case.

Step 7 — Replay a pointwise judge and keep an audit record

Run the same process on eight frozen replies. Each row gives a response ID, the exact candidate, whether its approved source is available, and three observations supplied by an independent policy reader. The observations describe the deadline, receipt, and any unsupported promise. They are inputs to the exercise. The code never tries to extract policy facts from free text.

Keep the saved verdicts and the final human decisions in separate dictionaries keyed by response ID. The main loop looks them up using the ID from the captured reply. The human label is used only for comparison. The automatic route first checks for a confirmed critical contradiction, then checks whether the saved judge verdict is usable. A list expression such as [r for r in audit if r["usable"]] selects just the records whose verdicts cleared the checks.

Read validate() as a check of the output format, anchor() as a check against the reviewed facts, and inspect() as the evidence check connecting them. None becomes null in JSON. Here an abstention is reported separately and contributes no numeric rating to agreement. The quote rule recognizes only the teaching packet’s refund clause and two exact spans within it. It checks whether the selected span supports the particular anchor. A verdict accepting both requirements needs the full clause in this exercise.

Open Python Editor

import json

policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
help_text = "Support can answer questions in Orders."
reference_answer = "You may request a refund within the published window."
rubric_version = "refund-guidance-v1"
history = "The customer said the item is an eligible unused online purchase."
question = "How long after delivery can I request a refund for this order, and what do I need?"
question_b = "Can I still request a refund for my unused online order 45 days after delivery?"
routes = {1: "REJECT", 2: "REVIEW", 3: "REVIEW", 4: "ACCEPT", 5: "ACCEPT", None: "REVIEW"}
fields = {"score", "decision", "reason", "evidence"}
deadline_span = "through calendar day 30 after delivery"
receipt_span = "with a valid receipt"
approved_spans = {policy, deadline_span, receipt_span}

cases = [
    ("A", "Request a refund with a valid receipt through calendar day 30 after delivery, including day 30.", True, "inclusive", "required", False),
    ("B", "You can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.", True, "wrong", "required", False),
    ("C", "You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.", True, "correct", "missing", False),
    ("D", "The valid receipt is needed, and delivery is the starting point for the 30-calendar-day refund request window.", True, "correct", "required", False),
    ("E", "Every eligible request is automatically approved within 30 calendar days of delivery if you show a valid receipt.", True, "correct", "required", True),
    ("F", "You can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.", False, "unclear", "unclear", False),
    ("G", "With a valid receipt you may request a refund up to and including calendar day 30 after delivery.", True, "inclusive", "required", False),
    ("H", "Ask for a refund within 30 calendar days of delivery and have your valid receipt.", True, "correct", "required", False),
]

saved = {
    "A": '{"score":5,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"Both requirements and inclusion of day 30 are explicit.","evidence":"Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."}',
    "B": '{"score":4,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"The reply states the correct window and mentions a receipt.","evidence":"through calendar day 30 after delivery"}',
    "C": '{"score":3,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"The receipt requirement is absent.","evidence":"with a valid receipt"}',
    "D": '{"score":4,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"Both requirements are present.","evidence":"Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."}',
    "E": '{"score":4,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"The store promises automatic approval.","evidence":"All eligible requests are automatically approved."}',
    "F": '{"score":null,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"The approved policy is missing.","evidence":""}',
    "G": '{"score":5',
    "H": '{"score":6,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"Both requirements are present.","evidence":"with a valid receipt"}',
}
human = {
    "A": 5, "B": 1, "C": 3, "D": 4, "E": 2, "F": None, "G": 5, "H": 4,
}

def validate(raw):
    try:
        verdict = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None, "JSON parse error"
    if not isinstance(verdict, dict) or set(verdict) != fields:
        return None, "schema fields"
    score = verdict["score"]
    if score is not None and (type(score) is not int or score not in routes):
        return None, "score outside schema"
    if verdict["decision"] != routes[score]:
        return None, "decision outside schema"
    if not isinstance(verdict["reason"], str) or not verdict["reason"].strip():
        return None, "reason outside schema"
    evidence = verdict["evidence"]
    if not isinstance(evidence, str) or (score is None and evidence != ""):
        return None, "evidence outside schema"
    if score is not None and not evidence.strip():
        return None, "evidence outside schema"
    return verdict, None

def anchor(source_available, deadline, receipt, promise):
    if not source_available:
        return None
    if deadline == "wrong" or receipt == "waived":
        return 1
    if "unclear" in (deadline, receipt):
        return None
    if promise:
        return 2
    facts = int(deadline in ("inclusive", "correct")) + int(receipt == "required")
    if facts == 0:
        return 2
    if facts == 1:
        return 3
    return 5 if deadline == "inclusive" else 4

def inspect(verdict, problem, source, expected, deadline, receipt):
    if problem:
        return "UNSCORABLE", problem
    score = verdict["score"]
    if expected is None and score is None:
        return "ABSTAINED", "source missing" if source is None else "facts ambiguous"
    if source is None:
        return "UNSCORABLE", "source missing"
    if score is None:
        return "UNSCORABLE", "unexpected abstention"
    if verdict["evidence"] not in approved_spans or verdict["evidence"] not in source:
        return "UNSCORABLE", "unsupported citation"
    if score != expected:
        return "UNSCORABLE", "rubric mismatch"
    relevant_span = policy
    if score == 1 and deadline == "wrong":
        relevant_span = deadline_span
    elif score == 1 and receipt == "waived":
        relevant_span = receipt_span
    elif score == 3:
        relevant_span = receipt_span if receipt == "missing" else deadline_span
    if verdict["evidence"] not in (policy, relevant_span):
        return "UNSCORABLE", "citation misses requirement"
    return "USABLE", "quote and anchor checked"

audit = []
for name, candidate, has_source, deadline, receipt, promise in cases:
    source = policy + "\n" + help_text if has_source else None
    expected = anchor(has_source, deadline, receipt, promise)
    verdict, problem = validate(saved[name])
    status, why = inspect(verdict, problem, source, expected, deadline, receipt)
    if expected == 1:
        decision = "REJECT"
    elif status == "USABLE":
        decision = routes[verdict["score"]]
    else:
        decision = "REVIEW"
    record = {
        "id": name, "question": question_b if name == "B" else question, "history": history,
        "candidate": candidate, "reference_example": reference_answer, "source": source,
        "policy_version": "refund-1" if has_source else None,
        "rubric_version": rubric_version, "raw_judge": saved[name], "judge_result": verdict,
        "reviewed_facts": (deadline, receipt, promise), "status": status, "reason": why,
        "candidate_decision": decision, "human_score": human[name],
    }
    audit.append(record)
    print(f"{name}: {status} ({why}) | candidate {decision} | human {human[name]}")

scored = [r for r in audit if r["status"] == "USABLE"]
checked = [r for r in scored if r["human_score"] is not None]
matches = sum(r["judge_result"]["score"] == r["human_score"] for r in checked)
print(f"Usable scores: {len(scored)}/{len(audit)} | matches with human: {matches}/{len(checked)}")
sample = audit[2]
print(f'Audit {sample["id"]} | policy {sample["policy_version"]} | rubric {sample["rubric_version"]}')
print(f'Candidate: {sample["candidate"]}')
print(f'Saved judge: {sample["raw_judge"]}')
Expected output
A: USABLE (quote and anchor checked) | candidate ACCEPT | human 5
B: UNSCORABLE (rubric mismatch) | candidate REJECT | human 1
C: USABLE (quote and anchor checked) | candidate REVIEW | human 3
D: USABLE (quote and anchor checked) | candidate ACCEPT | human 4
E: UNSCORABLE (unsupported citation) | candidate REVIEW | human 2
F: ABSTAINED (source missing) | candidate REVIEW | human None
G: UNSCORABLE (JSON parse error) | candidate REVIEW | human 5
H: UNSCORABLE (score outside schema) | candidate REVIEW | human 4
Usable scores: 3/8 | matches with human: 3/3
Audit C | policy refund-1 | rubric refund-guidance-v1
Candidate: You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.
Saved judge: {"score":3,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"The receipt requirement is absent.","evidence":"with a valid receipt"}

Experiment. In the saved dictionary, change only A's "score":5 to "score":4. A's decision field stays ACCEPT, which the schema permits for either rating.

Expected output
A: UNSCORABLE (rubric mismatch) | candidate REVIEW | human 5
B: UNSCORABLE (rubric mismatch) | candidate REJECT | human 1
C: USABLE (quote and anchor checked) | candidate REVIEW | human 3
D: USABLE (quote and anchor checked) | candidate ACCEPT | human 4
E: UNSCORABLE (unsupported citation) | candidate REVIEW | human 2
F: ABSTAINED (source missing) | candidate REVIEW | human None
G: UNSCORABLE (JSON parse error) | candidate REVIEW | human 5
H: UNSCORABLE (score outside schema) | candidate REVIEW | human 4
Usable scores: 2/8 | matches with human: 2/2
Audit C | policy refund-1 | rubric refund-guidance-v1
Candidate: You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.
Saved judge: {"score":3,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"The receipt requirement is absent.","evidence":"with a valid receipt"}

A still parses, uses an allowed score, and includes a real quote. The candidate explicitly includes day 30, so the reviewed facts require anchor 5. The altered verdict is unusable. The candidate stays intact and goes to review. B stays rejected on its independently verified deadline. D clears the refund-guidance criterion. A separate clarity check can still ask for a rewrite.

Checkpoint. Did the perfect fraction among checked verdicts mean the judge performed equally well on all replies? Review the coverage next to it. The denominator shrank because A's rating failed validation. This agreement is conditional on evidence and anchor checks, which use supplied human-reviewed facts. The exercise verifies a replay pipeline. It cannot estimate the reliability of a judge on unseen answers, and the narrow rule does not check whether every sentence in a free-text explanation is sound.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Fix a vague prompt

A judge receives the candidate “Ask within 30 days,” the approved refund clause, and the instruction “Rate this from 1 to 5.” List four pieces of instruction or context you would add. Explain how each helps the reviewer interpret the output.

Practice 2. Apply an anchor

Under refund-1, the candidate says “Keep your valid receipt. You may request your refund up to and including calendar day 30 after delivery.” Rate it for refund guidance. Now remove the receipt sentence and rate it again.

Practice 3. Read the quote against the claim

A judge accepts the 90-day answer and explains “the policy agrees with the candidate.” It quotes “through calendar day 30 after delivery.” Explain how the verdict can pass schema checks and still need to be rejected. Identify the additional check that would catch it.

Practice 4. Tell a failed verdict from an unresolved candidate

A reply gives the correct-looking 30-day and receipt information, but the approved policy is missing. The saved verdict is either {"score":null,"decision":"REVIEW","reason":"No approved policy.","evidence":""} or {"score":6,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"Looks right.","evidence":"30 days"}. Explain how to log each verdict and what should happen to the candidate.

Independent Assignment

Harbor Leaf asks whether the saved judge output can safely be used on the eight replies in Step 7. Use those captured questions and history, the approved refund clause when present, the frozen candidates, rubric, and replay outputs. First classify B, E, F, G, and H by hand. Then explain how each judge outcome differs from the action taken on the reply. Give a reviewer the audit row and say what evidence or corrected output they need next.

Use the full Step 7 program as the executable answer key. Copy it into a fresh editor for each variant. In variant A, replace G's truncated entry in saved with the valid verdict '{"score":5,"decision":"ACCEPT","reason":"Both requirements and inclusion of day 30 are explicit.","evidence":"Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."}'. In variant B, start again from the baseline and replace only E's invented evidence text with through calendar day 30 after delivery. Leave E's score and reason in place. Record the changed rows, usable score coverage, and agreement among checked usable scores.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Give the original question so the judge knows whether both requirements were asked for. Specify refund guidance as the only criterion so style does not dominate. Include the score anchors and the contradiction priority so a 3 or 1 has a shared meaning. Require the JSON fields and evidence rules, including how to abstain when information is missing. A reviewer can then distinguish the result from the justification and inspect both.

Solution 2

The first reply explicitly confirms day 30 and includes the receipt, so it meets anchor 5. The shortened reply still preserves the deadline and starting event. Its missing receipt leaves just one requirement, so it earns 3 and goes to review for revision.

Solution 3

The fields could all be present, and 4 and ACCEPT could be allowed together. The quote even appears in the approved text. Set the quoted 30 next to the candidate's 90. This verifies a contradiction that takes priority over other strengths. Log the judge verdict as unusable and reject the candidate by the independent check.

Solution 4

Write down what happened on two separate lines. The null verdict followed the instructions for missing evidence. Save it as an abstention and ask for the approved policy. The 6 verdict broke the scoring contract. Save the raw output and log an out-of-range score. Both candidate replies go to review. A support reviewer needs the official policy in either case, while the evaluator owner also needs to investigate the invalid rating.

Assignment answer key

B contradicts the deadline and can be independently rejected. E is unscorable because its quote was invented and requires review for an unsupported promise. F is a valid abstention and needs the policy. Reject G's unusable output at parsing and H's at schema validation. In both cases the candidate still needs a trustworthy check. Log the response ID, frozen text, policy and rubric versions, raw verdict, failure reason, final route, and human outcome on review.

For variant A, the only changed output lines are G: USABLE (quote and anchor checked) | candidate ACCEPT | human 5 and Usable scores: 4/8 | matches with human: 4/4. This repair supplies a readable verdict that matches the provided evidence and anchor for G.

For variant B, the only changed output line is E: UNSCORABLE (rubric mismatch) | candidate REVIEW | human 2. The genuine quote now passes the citation rule, but the answer still promises automatic approval, which the source does not support. The coverage line remains Usable scores: 3/8 | matches with human: 3/3. Ask a reviewer to inspect the claim and update the wording. Record why the verdict remains unusable.

Knowledge Check

  1. You rate replies A and B on the same scale in two separate calls. Is that pointwise judging even if you compare the scores later?
  2. The reference says “within the published window.” What would you provide to support a real judgment of the 30-day claim?
  3. Why does a crisp but incorrect 90-day reply get 1 even if it reads better than the approved example?
  4. Two judges disagree over whether “good” means polished or complete. Which instruction would you change first?
  5. JSON parses with a score of "3". Which check flags this and why?
  6. The judge quotes the exact receipt clause and says a candidate included it. The reply only mentions the deadline. How would you test that verdict?
  7. Two replays agree on 4 but a human looking at the same saved reply gives 1. Which evidence do you inspect?
  8. A verdict is malformed and there is no independent policy check yet. What belongs in the audit record and where should the candidate go?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Yes. Each call rates one candidate against its own inputs and the rubric. Comparing the resulting scores later is separate from asking a model to pick between two candidates.
  2. Supply the approved clause and version for this order, including that the 30 calendar days count from delivery. The example answer alone leaves that fact unstated.
  3. The rubric is about refund guidance. Its first anchor gives priority to an explicit contradiction. Score readability in a separate review.
  4. Name the criterion and rewrite “good” as observable requirements. Give an example showing the difference between a correct deadline alone and an answer that also includes the receipt.
  5. The schema check rejects it. JSON quotes turn the digit into text, while the numeric anchor requires an integer.
  6. The quote establishes the receipt requirement. Read the candidate for the receipt condition, and assign the omission anchor if the deadline is correct and no more serious issue is present.
  7. Line up the response ID, text, policy version, and rubric. Check the conflicting claim against the approved clause. Agreement between the replays is evidence about consistency only.
  8. Save the raw output alongside the case ID, question, candidate, rubric and source versions, and parsing error. Mark the verdict unscorable and route the candidate to review. Attach the reviewer’s outcome when available.

Common Mistakes

Keep the original candidate and policy version. If two reviewers rate different drafts, their score difference cannot isolate a judging problem.

Check the reason and its evidence as well as the rating. A genuine but irrelevant quote, a legitimate omission, and an explicit contradiction call for different actions.

Report abstentions and unusable verdicts beside agreement. Otherwise a report could look strong because it quietly counted only the cases that were easy to validate.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Pointwise judging applies a rubric to one saved response at a time. Keep each criterion clear, define what every rating looks like, and verify the verdict in layers. When the source or judgment is unusable, preserve the evidence and route the case for review. A verified policy contradiction can block the answer independently of the judge’s output.

Next, Human agreement, calibration and bias compares human and model labels across a set of saved cases.

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Match independent reviewer and judge labels to frozen response IDs and calculate exact agreement.
  • Use the approved policy to check whether agreement reflects a justified outcome.
  • Read a confusion matrix and calculate Cohen’s kappa from observed agreement and each reviewer’s label frequencies.
  • Clarify rubric anchors, investigate style preferences, and report held-out errors, sample sizes, and unresolved cases.

Why This Lesson Matters

Your parcel arrived 45 days ago. Harbor Leaf Market’s assistant tells you the store gives you 90 days to request a refund. Two reviewers and an automated judge approve the reply. Then someone opens the policy and finds a 30-day deadline. The customer is already too late. Before trusting the next round of ratings, the team needs to understand how three matching judgments missed the same fact.

The store, messages, labels, and replay outputs in this chapter are fictional. Policy refund-1 says “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included. Each customer in the fixture has an eligible unused online order and asks for the deadline and what they need to request a refund. The approved clause is the reference for those answers.

Allow about six hours. Start with Pointwise LLM-as-a-Judge. Annotation, adjudication and synthetic data and Sampling, holdouts, leakage and maintenance are recommended background. Use the latter before building your own calibration and holdout sets. This chapter supplies separate case IDs and replays so you can inspect both sets entirely offline.

Beginner Explanation

Start with two independent reads

Nia and Omar each receive the same policy, question, and saved replies. They record their labels without seeing each other’s work or the judge’s output. This is independent review. A rubric is their shared scoring guide. Version v1 says PASS for “sufficient refund guidance,” FAIL for wrong or insufficient guidance, and REVIEW for a material doubt. It does not say clearly whether omitting the receipt makes a reply insufficient. A rubric anchor is a concrete example showing which label to assign and why.

Preparation skills
IDFrozen replyNiaOmarJudge replay v1
AYou may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.PASSPASSPASS
BYou can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.PASSPASSPASS
CAsk for a refund during the first month after delivery if you have proof of purchase.REVIEWPASSPASS
DYou can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.FAILPASSPASS
EContact our support team for assistance.FAILFAILFAIL

Put a check mark next to each row where Nia and Omar gave the same label. You’ll mark A and B for matching PASS labels, and E for matching FAIL labels. C and D get no mark. You have three marks across five rows that both people rated. Divide 3 by 5 to get 60%. That is exact agreement. It counts matches, so on a five-point scale a 4 versus a 5 is a mismatch just as a 1 versus a 5 is.

The judge matches Nia on three cases and Omar on all five. Nia and Omar use different interpretations of the receipt rule. Matching one person more often does not tell you whose interpretation is supported. Check each disagreement using the frozen reply and the source. Then inspect some agreements too. B is where all three labels miss the same fact.

Confirm what the policy supports

Put B’s “90 calendar days” beside the approved “through calendar day 30.” At day 45, the two statements give different instructions. The written policy provides stronger evidence than the three matching labels. An independent reviewer can now record FAIL for this specific claim.

A person who resolves a disputed judgment by reading the evidence and applying an agreed rule is doing adjudication. Keep their reason alongside their decision. For D, the updated rubric can make the omission rule explicit and support FAIL. For C, there is no exact day count and no clear confirmation of a valid receipt. Leave its adjudicated label open and route it for clarification. REVIEW describes the next action. A pending reference means the team has yet to establish a binary outcome for this report.

Report judge agreement with each reviewer separately. Then compare valid judge labels against adjudicated labels when available. The second comparison estimates correctness against a documented reference on those cases. A reference label is as trustworthy as the evidence and rule used to establish it. A judge output that cannot be read under the required format is invalid. In Step 7 that format is one label, so the illustrative raw value “{broken” cannot be scored. Keep it out of agreement and report it separately.

Read the types of mistakes

Imagine testing a held-out group with two adjudicated PASS cases and two adjudicated FAIL cases. The saved judge gets one of each right. Write the reference labels down the side and judge labels across the top. This count table is a confusion matrix.

Course hours by track
Adjudicated labelJudge PASSJudge FAIL
PASS11
FAIL11

The PASS/PASS and FAIL/FAIL cells give 2 matches out of 4. The FAIL row has one false pass out of two known FAIL replies. The PASS row has one false fail out of two known PASS replies. A judge that passes every reply can look strong on a set dominated by correct replies. Read each row before trusting the total. Report the number of cases, the number with both valid binary labels, and the cases excluded because of missing or invalid evidence.

Notice how the choice of labels affects agreement

Picture eight new refund replies. Nia and Omar both use PASS six times and FAIL twice. They match on six replies, giving observed agreement of 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75. If you shuffled each reviewer’s labels independently while keeping their label counts, you would still expect many PASS labels to land together. The expected agreement under this independence calculation is the product of the two PASS frequencies plus the product of the two FAIL frequencies. Here it is (6/8 × 6/8) + (2/8 × 2/8) = 0.625.

Cohen’s kappa compares the observed agreement to that baseline. The observed result is 0.75 − 0.625 = 0.125 above it. The best possible agreement is 1, so the available room was 1 − 0.625 = 0.375. Divide 0.125 by 0.375 to get 0.333. In symbols, κ = (observed − expected) ÷ (1 − expected). A kappa of 0 means the match rate equals this baseline. A negative value means fewer matches than the baseline expects. If expected agreement is 1, kappa is undefined. Cohen, A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales

If both reviewers used PASS and FAIL equally often with the same 75% observed agreement, expected agreement would be 0.50, and kappa would be 0.50. The frequency of a category in the set is its prevalence. Show the label counts, sample size, raw agreement, and kappa together. Kappa describes agreement under a particular baseline. It cannot tell you whether either person applied the refund policy correctly.

Calibrate the rule, then test it on fresh cases

Choose practice cases that cover clear answers, wrong deadlines, missing receipts, and ambiguous replies. Have the reviewers label them independently. Compare their ratings and read the disputed text against the policy. Write down which part of the guide caused the disagreement. For instance, replace “sufficient refund guidance” with examples of a complete answer, a missing receipt, and an uncertain date. Save the resolved labels and any pending cases alongside a new rubric version. This is calibration in this lesson.

Keep a separate set for evaluation. A holdout is a set you keep away from the examples used to revise the rubric or judge prompt. Keep near-duplicate replies from the same question family in the same partition. Reviewers can prepare reference labels independently, while the people revising the rubric avoid reading the holdout cases or scores until the rules are frozen. Opening the same outcomes after each edit lets you tailor the rule to those particular replies. Using held-out examples to pick a rule moves information into the design process. That is data leakage. If you revise the rules after reading the results, treat those cases as development evidence and use a fresh holdout.

Test a suspected preference without changing the facts

Take a correct short reply and a longer version with the same facts. Give both the same question, policy, rubric, and judge settings. If the longer wording repeatedly gets a better verdict, investigate a possible preference for verbosity. Try adding “Definitely” to a wrong reply to test confidence. Show the same two policy facts once in a paragraph and once as a numbered list to test formatting. Compare a plain reply with a polished paraphrase that keeps the deadline and receipt unchanged. Change one property at a time. Keep the review focused on the refund requirements unless the rubric explicitly includes style. A slice is a subgroup, such as short or long replies, whose errors you report separately.

An evaluator may also favor replies generated by its own model family. This is model self-preference. For example, the judge may pass its own model family’s replies more often than equally accurate replies written by another family. Keep model identities hidden when possible and compare independently labeled examples from several sources. Check whether the pattern persists after matching on facts and controlling presentation. If you present multiple answers together, their order may affect judgments. Here each replay rates one reply independently. For pointwise repeat consistency, rerun that same reply with the same inputs and count how often the verdict changes. Repeat agreement can coexist with a repeated mistake. Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

A report should keep each case ID, frozen reply, policy, dataset version, split, reviewer IDs and labels, raw judge output, rubric version, disagreement reason, adjudicated outcome, and calibration action. Include the counts and denominators behind each summary. Save each new run alongside the earlier one. This report computes agreement from the saved per-case labels so a colleague can reproduce the calculation.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Count the matches before asking why

User question. How long after delivery can I ask for a refund, and what do I need?

Approved reference. Under refund-1 the window ends on calendar day 30 and a valid receipt is required.

Actual LLM response. D says “You can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.” Read D with A, B, C, and E in the calibration table.

Assessment. Nia and Omar each labeled all five replies separately. A, B, and E match, giving 3/5 or 60% agreement. C and D differ. On D, Omar treated the deadline as sufficient guidance, while Nia considered the receipt a required part of the answer.

Failure classification. Keep both original labels. Record an omission under the clarified rubric and add an anchor that names the missing receipt as a failure for this question. The 60% describes this table and cannot explain the disagreement by itself.

Example 2. Find an error inside unanimous agreement

User question. How long after delivery can I request a refund, and what do I need?

Approved reference. The approved source allows a request through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.

Actual LLM response. B says “You can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.”

Assessment. Nia, Omar, and the judge replay all use PASS. Read the cutoff directly from the reply and the source. At day 45, B says the request is within the window, but the approved clause says the window has ended. Record an adjudicated FAIL under the same ID.

Failure classification. Write two lines for B. On the agreement line, all three pairs of raters matched: Nia and Omar, Nia and the judge, Omar and the judge. On the policy line, all three PASS labels conflict with the 30-day rule. Keep the original labels, block the reply, and record the evidence for FAIL. Use B in calibration to show why a similar format and a correct receipt condition cannot rescue a wrong deadline.

Example 3. Investigate which answers earned undeserved credit

User question. For the same eligible order, how long do I have and what do I need to request a refund?

Approved reference. Use refund-1. A PASS answers both required facts. A wrong deadline is FAIL even when the answer is polished.

Actual LLM response. The frozen holdout has F and G, short and long versions of a correct answer for a blender order, and H and I, short and long versions of the same wrong 90-day answer for a jacket order. J is ambiguous. K has an invalid replay output. The exact texts and outputs are in Step 7.

Assessment. The first replay labels F and H FAIL and G and I PASS. Among comparable cases it scores 1/2 on short replies and 1/2 on long replies. The short error is a false fail and the long error is a false pass. Revise the prompt on the separate calibration set, then check saved holdout outputs for the revised guide. The fictional replay changes F to PASS and I to FAIL and leaves G and H correct. Comparable cases rise from two correct out of four to four out of four. J and K stay outside that comparison.

Failure classification. The first replay is consistent with a possible length preference on these pairs. The second reduces the observed errors in this teaching set. Keep the two runs, fixtures, and evidence notes linked to their versions. Test the pattern on more matched examples before claiming a general preference or better performance from a live judge.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Select Copy Code, open the editor next to the program, paste the full block, and select Run. Check the first output before making the one specified change. Each activity starts in a fresh editor, uses inline data, and runs on standard Python. The human and judge labels are fictional saved records. The programs calculate comparisons and never call a model.

Step 1 — Compare two human reviewers by response ID

Match the labels for the same frozen reply before counting agreements. The list holds tuples, ordered groups of three values. The for line gives those values names in the order they appear. == tests whether two labels are equal. The conditional expression picks “match” if the labels agree and “disagree” otherwise.

Open Python Editor

rows = [
    ("A", "PASS", "PASS"),
    ("B", "PASS", "PASS"),
    ("C", "REVIEW", "PASS"),
    ("D", "FAIL", "PASS"),
    ("E", "FAIL", "FAIL"),
]

for case_id, nia, omar in rows:
    result = "match" if nia == omar else "disagree"
    print(f"{case_id}: Nia {nia} | Omar {omar} | {result}")
Expected output
A: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
B: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
C: Nia REVIEW | Omar PASS | disagree
D: Nia FAIL | Omar PASS | disagree
E: Nia FAIL | Omar FAIL | match

Experiment. In D’s row only, change Omar’s label, the last value, from PASS to FAIL.

Expected output
A: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
B: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
C: Nia REVIEW | Omar PASS | disagree
D: Nia FAIL | Omar FAIL | match
E: Nia FAIL | Omar FAIL | match

The D comparison changes because both labels are now FAIL. Checkpoint. Which input would justify that change in an actual review? Record the missing receipt alongside the rubric rule, and keep Omar’s earlier label. This experiment changes a copy of a rating.

Step 2 — Calculate exact agreement

Count matches out of all comparable pairs in the first table. In this activity REVIEW counts as a recorded label, and every case has both ratings. When Python adds comparisons with sum(), each True counts as one. len() counts pairs. In an f"..." string, :.1f displays one decimal place.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [("PASS", "PASS"), ("PASS", "PASS"), ("REVIEW", "PASS"),
         ("FAIL", "PASS"), ("FAIL", "FAIL")]
matches = sum(nia == omar for nia, omar in pairs)
total = len(pairs)

print(f"Matches: {matches}/{total}")
print(f"Exact agreement: {100 * matches / total:.1f}%")
Expected output
Matches: 3/5
Exact agreement: 60.0%

Experiment. Change Omar’s PASS to FAIL only in the pair ("FAIL", "PASS").

Expected output
Matches: 4/5
Exact agreement: 80.0%

One additional pair matches and the denominator stays five. Checkpoint. Does removing a disputed row give the same result? Removing D instead would give 3/4, or 75%, on a different set. Document exclusions rather than using them to raise the headline percentage.

Step 3 — Compare the judge with each human

Use the fictional v1 judge labels. Each dictionary stores labels keyed by case ID, so judge[case_id] retrieves the matching row regardless of insertion order. Loop over the reviewer IDs and compare all five cases.

Open Python Editor

nia = {"A": "PASS", "B": "PASS", "C": "REVIEW", "D": "FAIL", "E": "FAIL"}
omar = {"A": "PASS", "B": "PASS", "C": "PASS", "D": "PASS", "E": "FAIL"}
judge = {"A": "PASS", "B": "PASS", "C": "PASS", "D": "PASS", "E": "FAIL"}

for reviewer, labels in [("Nia", nia), ("Omar", omar)]:
    matches = sum(judge[case_id] == labels[case_id] for case_id in labels)
    print(f"Judge vs {reviewer}: {matches}/{len(labels)} ({100 * matches / len(labels):.1f}%)")
Expected output
Judge vs Nia: 3/5 (60.0%)
Judge vs Omar: 5/5 (100.0%)

Experiment. In judge, change C from PASS to REVIEW.

Expected output
Judge vs Nia: 4/5 (80.0%)
Judge vs Omar: 4/5 (80.0%)

Look at C’s row after the edit. The judge gains one match with Nia and loses one with Omar. Both totals land at four, but nobody changed the customer’s reply or found new policy evidence. Checkpoint. Which result tells you what “first month” means for the customer? Neither match count answers that. Give an adjudicator the frozen reply and the applicable policy so they can check the date and receipt wording.

Step 4 — Check the claim behind a unanimous label

Compare a controlled teaching reply with the policy. Both versions use calendar days after delivery and include the receipt, so the direct rule can check the exact number. all() returns true when every comparison is true. The numbers in the program are supplied inline. It does not extract facts from chat text.

Open Python Editor

policy_days = 30
stated_days = 30
labels = ["PASS", "PASS", "PASS"]
reference = "PASS" if stated_days == policy_days else "FAIL"

print(f"Reply: Refund requests are allowed through day {stated_days} after delivery with a valid receipt.")
print(f"Unanimous: {all(label == labels[0] for label in labels)}")
print(f"Checked deadline: {reference}")
print(f"Labels matching the deadline check: {labels.count(reference)}/{len(labels)}")
Expected output
Reply: Refund requests are allowed through day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Unanimous: True
Checked deadline: PASS
Labels matching the deadline check: 3/3

Experiment. Change only stated_days = 30 to stated_days = 90. This controlled example holds old labels fixed to show how consensus can hide an error.

Expected output
Reply: Refund requests are allowed through day 90 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Unanimous: True
Checked deadline: FAIL
Labels matching the deadline check: 0/3

All three labels still match each other. The number contradicts the policy. Checkpoint. What would you do with the saved labels in a real audit? Keep them with the exact reply they were recorded against, and add a new evidence-backed decision for that reply. Never attach old ratings to an edited response as though they had reviewed it.

Step 5 — Adjust agreement for label frequency

Use the eight fresh examples from the kappa calculation. The four counts say how often each pair of labels occurred. The sum gives the number of pairs. Divide the row and column totals by that number to find each reviewer’s label frequencies. Multiply matching frequencies to get expected agreement, then subtract it from observed agreement before dividing by the remaining room.

Open Python Editor

both_pass = 5
nia_pass_omar_fail = 1
nia_fail_omar_pass = 1
both_fail = 1

total = both_pass + nia_pass_omar_fail + nia_fail_omar_pass + both_fail
observed = (both_pass + both_fail) / total
nia_pass = (both_pass + nia_pass_omar_fail) / total
omar_pass = (both_pass + nia_fail_omar_pass) / total
expected = nia_pass * omar_pass + (1 - nia_pass) * (1 - omar_pass)

print(f"Observed agreement: {observed:.3f}")
print(f"Expected agreement: {expected:.4f}")
if expected == 1:
    print("Kappa: undefined")
else:
    print(f"Kappa: {(observed - expected) / (1 - expected):.3f}")
Expected output
Observed agreement: 0.750
Expected agreement: 0.6250
Kappa: 0.333

Experiment. Reassign one pair from Nia FAIL/Omar PASS to both FAIL, leaving eight cases. Replace the four consecutive count assignments with both_pass, nia_pass_omar_fail, nia_fail_omar_pass, both_fail = 5, 1, 0, 2.

Expected output
Observed agreement: 0.875
Expected agreement: 0.5625
Kappa: 0.714

The reassignment keeps Nia at six PASS labels and moves Omar from six to five. The two expected contributions become 30/64 and 6/64. Observed agreement is 7/8, so kappa is (0.875 − 0.5625) ÷ 0.4375 ≈ 0.714. Checkpoint. If both reviewers use only PASS, what does the program print? Expected agreement becomes 1, so kappa is undefined even with unanimous PASS. Record the raw counts and inspect the sample mix.

Step 6 — Look for a preference on matched replies

Replay the fictional judge on two matched pairs from Harbor Leaf. Within each pair, the short and long reply state the same facts. One pair is correct and the other gives the wrong deadline. Count the number of times the long version alone passes. The word counts help identify the style contrast. The final tally uses three saved runs for F. It uses the first as the comparison label and counts the first run as a match, so one of the two subsequent runs differs.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [
    ("correct", "With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 30 from delivery.",
     "For an eligible order, please make your request within 30 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
     "FAIL", "PASS"),
    ("wrong deadline", "With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 90 from delivery.",
     "For an eligible order, please make your request within 90 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
     "FAIL", "PASS"),
]
long_only = 0
for case, short, long, short_label, long_label in pairs:
    long_only += short_label == "FAIL" and long_label == "PASS"
    print(f"{case}: short {len(short.split())} words {short_label} | long {len(long.split())} words {long_label}")

repeats_f = ["FAIL", "PASS", "FAIL"]
matches = repeats_f.count(repeats_f[0])
print(f"Long-only passes: {long_only}/{len(pairs)}")
print(f"F repeats matching the first verdict: {matches}/{len(repeats_f)}")
Expected output
correct: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words PASS
wrong deadline: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words PASS
Long-only passes: 2/2
F repeats matching the first verdict: 2/3

Experiment. In the pair named "wrong deadline", change only the final judge label from "PASS" to "FAIL".

Expected output
correct: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words PASS
wrong deadline: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words FAIL
Long-only passes: 1/2
F repeats matching the first verdict: 2/3

The judge now fails both versions of the wrong answer. The correct pair still shows a style-related difference, and the separate repeat tally stays fixed. Checkpoint. Can two pairs isolate length as the cause? The long drafts also change sentence structure. Try more matched paraphrases and vary formatting, confidence, and length separately before attributing a pattern.

Step 7 — Replay the calibration and audit report

Use frozen cases and two dictionaries of fictional replay labels. Each key is a case ID. A through E were available during calibration. F through K are the holdout. Both replay versions use identical candidate texts and independent human ratings. The fictional v2 guide explicitly requires the deadline and receipt, fails contradictions and material omissions, sends ambiguity to REVIEW, and asks the judge to ignore tone and length. The v2 labels are supplied for comparison. The Python code does not generate them.

Each case row contains the reply, style, two original human labels, a reviewed day count when available, and any adjudicated binary label. F/G and H/I share a ticket within each pair. The ticket check keeps both versions of each answer in the same split. A reason is stored even when adjudication remains pending. set(calibration_ids).isdisjoint(holdout_ids) checks that no ID belongs to both groups. A set comparison checks that all cases are assigned. In the report, the tuple key (reference, judge) keeps the two axes of the confusion matrix in that order.

For judge-human agreement, a valid REVIEW counts as a label when comparing raw ratings. For the binary confusion matrix, a case needs both an adjudicated PASS or FAIL and a valid judge PASS or FAIL. Missing sources, unresolved references, valid judge abstentions, and malformed verdicts need their own counts or reasons. The policy check uses day counts already checked for unit and starting event. The omitted receipt on D is recorded in the adjudicator’s note.

# Text, style, Nia, Omar, verified day count, adjudicated label, evidence note.
cases = {
    "A": ("You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
    "B": ("You can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 90, "FAIL", "deadline contradicts policy"),
    "C": ("Ask for a refund during the first month after delivery if you have proof of purchase.",
          "short", "REVIEW", "PASS", None, None, "date and receipt wording need clarification"),
    "D": ("You can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.",
          "short", "FAIL", "PASS", 30, "FAIL", "receipt omitted"),
    "E": ("Contact our support team for assistance.",
          "short", "FAIL", "FAIL", None, "FAIL", "neither requested fact stated"),
    "F": ("With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 30 from delivery.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
    "G": ("For an eligible order, please make your request within 30 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
          "long", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
    "H": ("With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 90 from delivery.",
          "short", "FAIL", "FAIL", 90, "FAIL", "deadline contradicts policy"),
    "I": ("For an eligible order, please make your request within 90 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
          "long", "FAIL", "PASS", 90, "FAIL", "deadline contradicts policy"),
    "J": ("Bring a valid receipt and apply within thirty days of placing or receiving the order, whichever date applies.",
          "short", "REVIEW", "REVIEW", None, None, "starting event for the 30 days is unclear"),
    "K": ("With a valid receipt, you can ask for a refund up to and including day 30 after delivery.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
}
replays = {
    "v1": dict(zip("ABCDEFGHIJK", ("PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "FAIL",
                                    "FAIL", "PASS", "FAIL", "PASS", "PASS", "{broken"))),
    "v2": dict(zip("ABCDEFGHIJK", ("PASS", "FAIL", "REVIEW", "FAIL", "FAIL",
                                    "PASS", "PASS", "FAIL", "FAIL", "REVIEW", "{broken"))),
}

assert set(calibration_ids).isdisjoint(holdout_ids)
calibration_tickets = {ticket.get(case_id, case_id) for case_id in calibration_ids}
holdout_tickets = {ticket.get(case_id, case_id) for case_id in holdout_ids}
assert calibration_tickets.isdisjoint(holdout_tickets)
assert set(calibration_ids) | set(holdout_ids) == set(cases) == set(replays[rubric])
audit = {}
for case_id, (reply, style, nia, omar, days, reference, note) in cases.items():
    raw_judge = replays[rubric][case_id]
    judge = raw_judge if raw_judge in labels else None
    gate = "UNKNOWN" if days is None else ("PASS" if days == 30 else "FAIL")
    assert gate != "FAIL" or reference == "FAIL"
    audit[case_id] = {
        "id": case_id, "dataset": dataset, "policy_version": "refund-1", "source": policy,
        "rubric": rubric, "split": "calibration" if case_id in calibration_ids else "holdout",
        "ticket": ticket.get(case_id, case_id),
        "question": holdout_questions.get(ticket.get(case_id, case_id), question),
        "candidate": reply, "style": style, "Nia": nia, "Omar": omar,
        "raw_judge": raw_judge, "judge": judge, "deadline_check": gate,
        "adjudicated": reference, "reference_note": note,
        "human_dispute": nia != omar,
        "calibration_action": "add anchors for deadline, receipt, and ambiguity",
    }

print(f"{dataset} | rubric {rubric}")
for group, ids in [("Calibration", calibration_ids), ("Holdout", holdout_ids)]:
    rows = [audit[case_id] for case_id in ids]
    valid = [r for r in rows if r["judge"] is not None]
    comparable = [r for r in valid if r["adjudicated"] in binary and r["judge"] in binary]
    human_matches = sum(r["Nia"] == r["Omar"] for r in rows)
    judge_nia = sum(r["judge"] == r["Nia"] for r in valid)
    judge_omar = sum(r["judge"] == r["Omar"] for r in valid)
    matches = sum(r["judge"] == r["adjudicated"] for r in comparable)
    unresolved = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["adjudicated"] is None]
    invalid = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["judge"] is None]
    disputes = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["human_dispute"]]
    print(f"{group} n={len(rows)}: human {human_matches}/{len(rows)} | judge vs Nia {judge_nia}/{len(valid)} | judge vs Omar {judge_omar}/{len(valid)}")
    print(f"  valid {len(valid)}/{len(rows)} | adjudicated matches {matches}/{len(comparable)}")
    print(f"  disputed {','.join(disputes)} | unresolved {','.join(unresolved)} | invalid {','.join(invalid) or 'none'}")
    if group == "Holdout":
        matrix = {(ref, pred): 0 for ref in binary for pred in binary}
        for r in comparable:
            matrix[r["adjudicated"], r["judge"]] += 1
        for ref in binary:
            print(f"  ref {ref}: judge PASS {matrix[ref, 'PASS']} | judge FAIL {matrix[ref, 'FAIL']}")
        for ref, pred, error in [("FAIL", "PASS", "False passes"), ("PASS", "FAIL", "False fails")]:
            total = sum(matrix[ref, label] for label in binary)
            count = matrix[ref, pred]
            rate = f"{count}/{total} ({100 * count / total:.1f}%)" if total else "unavailable (0 comparable)"
            print(f"  {error}: {rate}")
        for style in ("short", "long"):
            members = [r for r in comparable if r["style"] == style]
            correct = sum(r["judge"] == r["adjudicated"] for r in members)
            print(f"  {style}: {correct}/{len(members)} adjudicated matches")

for case_id in ("B", "I"):

    print(f"Audit {case_id}: refund-1 | deadline {r['deadline_check']} | judge {r['judge']} | adjudicated {r['adjudicated']} | {r['reference_note']}")

Could you report perfect held-out reliability? You can report four matches among four comparable teaching cases, with two cases outside that comparison and five valid judge outputs in six attempts.
