Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Read the ratings before calculating

From A through E, list the cases where Nia and Omar agree. For the remaining cases, write what would need to be checked to resolve the difference. Explain why B deserves a policy check even if no one flagged it.

Practice 2. Compare two denominators

On five replies, both reviewers label three identically. One reviewer then withdraws the label on one of the two disputed replies pending evidence. Compute agreement first on all five recorded pairs and then on the four remaining comparable pairs. How should the report describe the change?

Practice 3. Find the false pass

A saved judge and both reviewers pass a 90-day reply. The approved policy states 30 calendar days after delivery. The holdout also includes another known FAIL that the judge fails, and two known PASS replies, one of which the judge fails. Fill the four confusion-matrix cells and calculate the false-pass and false-fail rates.

Practice 4. Design a calibration comparison

A judge passes a short correct reply and a long correct reply. For a wrong deadline, it fails the short version and passes the long version. A colleague concludes it is biased toward length. Explain what the four results support. Propose a revised anchor and a held-out comparison that could test the hypothesis while controlling for the facts.

Independent Assignment

Harbor Leaf wants an audit of the holdout report. Include human agreement, judge agreement with each reviewer, adjudicated agreement, class-specific errors, short and long style slices, unresolved cases, and invalid outputs. Use the policy, frozen candidates, human ratings, and two replay versions in Step 7. First reconcile A through E by hand. Then explain why both B and I are wrong when the replay says PASS. For C and J, write what would need clarification. For K, explain why the raw verdict cannot be counted as a substantive disagreement.

Use the full Step 7 program as the runnable answer key. Copy it afresh for each variant. In both variants choose rubric = "v2". In variant A, simulate a successful new replay for K by changing just the last value of the v2 tuple from "{broken" to "PASS". In variant B, use the original v2 tuple and change I, the ninth verdict, from "FAIL" to "PASS". In a real audit, save the retry or changed judge run separately. Tabulate what changed and recommend a calibration action backed by the policy and the disagreement pattern.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

A, B, and E match. Check whether C’s wording fixes the exact day, starting event, and valid receipt requirement before choosing a binary label. For D, confirm that the question asks for both requirements. The receipt is missing, so the clarified rubric records FAIL for the omission. B did not trigger a human dispute. Comparing 90 with the approved 30 reveals why a policy check is still needed on agreements.

Solution 2

Before the withdrawal, there are 3 matches out of 5 pairs, or 60%. With one disagreement missing a rating, three of four comparable pairs match, or 75%. Record both the change in agreement and the decrease in coverage from 5/5 to 4/5. No rating was improved by removing a row. The case still needs evidence.

Solution 3

Put one in each matrix cell. Of the two adjudicated FAIL replies, one was passed and one was failed. The false-pass rate is 1/2, or 50%. Of the two adjudicated PASS replies, one was passed and one was failed. The false-fail rate is also 1/2, or 50%. The policy, rather than the three matching judgments, establishes which row contains the 90-day reply.

Solution 4

Start with the two 90-day replies. Both give the same wrong deadline, and only the longer one passed. That is a reason to investigate. To make the next check fair, write a rule that says an explicitly wrong deadline earns FAIL. Set aside new pairs with the same day count, starting event, and receipt requirement in both versions. Change length first. Record how often wrong answers pass, then try separate changes to tone or formatting. If the long answers add a missing policy fact, the comparison can no longer tell you what length contributed.

Assignment answer key

The calibration human agreement is 3/5. In v1 the judge agrees with Nia on 3/5 and Omar on 5/5. B’s 90-day claim contradicts the source on the calibration set. I independently makes the same mistake in the holdout. C needs a definite date and proof that the receipt condition is covered. J needs the answer to name delivery as the start of the window. K’s malformed verdict needs a retry and remains outside the binary matrix until a valid rating is available.

For variant A, the changed lines from v2 are Holdout n=6: human 5/6 | judge vs Nia 6/6 | judge vs Omar 5/6, valid 6/6 | adjudicated matches 5/5, disputed I | unresolved J | invalid none, ref PASS: judge PASS 3 | judge FAIL 0, False fails: 0/3 (0.0%), and short: 3/3 adjudicated matches. Indent the lines after the heading with two spaces, as in the report. The retry increases valid coverage without resolving J.

For variant B, the changed lines from v2 are Holdout n=6: human 5/6 | judge vs Nia 4/5 | judge vs Omar 5/5, valid 5/6 | adjudicated matches 3/4, ref FAIL: judge PASS 1 | judge FAIL 1, False passes: 1/2 (50.0%), long: 1/2 adjudicated matches, and Audit I: refund-1 | deadline FAIL | judge PASS | adjudicated FAIL | deadline contradicts policy. Indent the summary rows under Holdout as before. The judge now agrees perfectly with Omar on valid holdout outputs while making a confirmed policy error. Keep the contradiction anchor and investigate the long incorrect replies on separate paired examples. Keep unresolved and invalid cases visible in both variants.

Knowledge Check

  1. Omar sees Nia’s labels before recording his own. What does a high match rate fail to tell you about their independent judgment?
  2. Six of eight comparable ratings match. What is exact agreement, and does it describe how far mismatched scores were apart?
  3. All reviewers pass a 90-day reply and the policy gives 30. What action follows from each piece of evidence?
  4. Why can agreement with one reviewer go down after a rubric change while agreement with the adjudicated labels goes up?
  5. Both reviewers always say PASS. What happens to raw agreement and kappa, and what would you check next?
  6. A longer version gets PASS, but it added the valid-receipt requirement. Is this enough evidence of verbosity bias?
  7. You see a holdout result and revise the prompt specifically to fix it. What should you call that set now?
  8. The judge’s verdict is corrupt for K. A human reference is known. How does that affect coverage, agreement, and the audit record?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Omar may have been influenced by the visible marks. Preserve independent rating conditions so their match rate reflects separately reached decisions.
  2. It is 6/8, or 75%. Exact agreement counts every unequal pair once and does not encode the size of an ordinal difference.
  3. The unanimous rating tells you the reviewers and judge gave the same label. The documented rule supports a FAIL for the reply. Record the adjudication and investigate the shared miss.
  4. One reviewer may have treated the old ambiguous language as permission to overlook a missing receipt. A clearer rule can move the judge away from that reviewer and closer to evidence-backed decisions.
  5. Raw agreement is 100%. Expected agreement is 1, so kappa is undefined. Check whether the case mix includes instructive FAIL examples and independently verify the approved criteria.
  6. The extra receipt changes the factual content. To investigate length, keep policy facts fixed within each pair before rewriting style.
  7. Call the exposed cases development evidence and keep a new set sealed for evaluation. Retain the earlier result and connect each later run to its own prompt and data version.
  8. Count a failed attempt in coverage, but omit the invalid output from substantive agreement and the matrix. Store the raw output, case ID, verdict failure reason, and retry or review action.

Common Mistakes

Read some cases where everyone agreed. Shared assumptions or an overlooked fact can make all three labels wrong together.

Keep REVIEW, an unresolved reference, and an invalid judge output visible. Each has a different implication for the next action and the denominator.

Record which texts, reviewers, policy, and rubric produced each result. Keep calibration and holdout groups separate, and preserve earlier judgments when a new rubric changes the decision.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Match saved labels by response ID, read the policy to adjudicate, and report agreement beside validity coverage and error counts. Use kappa to understand how label frequencies affect the agreement baseline. Test suspected style preferences on controlled pairs and check rubric revisions on fresh cases before changing how the judge is used.

Next, Pairwise comparisons and ranking compares two answers at a time and checks what changes when their order is reversed.

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Apply a policy-first rubric when comparing two saved answers.
  • Record a winner, a tie, or a request for review and map display choices back to stable response IDs.
  • Replay each pair in reverse order, preserve disagreements, and count a supported pair once.
  • Build a win/loss/tie table and explain how coverage, cycles, and judge disagreement limit a ranking.
  • Explain the intuition behind Bradley–Terry and when a ranking still needs a separate factual check.

Why This Lesson Matters

Your Harbor Leaf Market parcel arrived 45 days ago. One draft says you still have time to request a refund because it allows 90 days. The other gives the store’s real 30-day deadline and asks for a receipt. If you’re reviewing the drafts side by side, the policy gives you a clear reason to choose. The harder question comes when two drafts get the facts right and the reviewer still has to decide whether either one is better.

All responses, sources, judges, and outcomes in this chapter are fictional. We keep the earlier Harbor Leaf policy refund-1: “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included. Assume an eligible unused online purchase throughout. The saved question is “Can I get a refund for something I bought?” Four fictional systems produced one frozen reply each. The judge sees display slots, and the report uses stable IDs A through D to track the replies.

Allow about 5.5 hours. The required background is Rubrics and a first human evaluation. Pointwise LLM-as-a-Judge and Human agreement, calibration and bias help with evidence and judge disagreement. Complete the pointwise lesson first if you add a live judge later. This lesson uses offline replays only.

Beginner Explanation

Compare the same answers in two ways
Course hours by track
Stable IDFrozen response
AYes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
BAbsolutely. You have 90 calendar days after delivery to request a refund, and a receipt is optional.
CBring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.
DPlease contact customer support about refunds.

Give A to a reviewer on its own. Ask whether it states the deadline, the starting event, and the receipt rule correctly. This is pointwise evaluation. It answers an absolute question such as whether a reply passes a policy check.

Now put A beside B and ask which reply gives the customer better refund guidance. This is pairwise evaluation. It can be easier to see why one draft is better than to decide whether a draft deserves 3 or 4 on a scale. The two approaches answer different questions. A reply can win a recorded preference and still fail the independent policy check.

Write the rule before showing the pair

Give both candidates the same saved question, approved policy, and rubric. Give the judge the same instructions in every position under rubric pairwise-v1 and ask it to return A, B, TIE, or REVIEW, plus a brief reason quoting the relevant reply and policy words. In this output format A and B are display slots. Keep the stable candidate IDs in the audit record, where they remain the same between displays.

  • Correctness first. A reply that follows the policy wins over one with a confirmed critical contradiction. Check the exact number, calendar-day unit, delivery event, and receipt requirement.
  • Completeness next. When the two replies preserve the facts, prefer the one that answers more of the question. A generic referral can avoid giving wrong advice while leaving the requested guidance missing.
  • Clarity and conciseness last. Compare how easy the replies are to follow and whether extra words help the customer. A confident tone or polished formatting cannot rescue a wrong rule.
  • TIE means you compared both answers with sufficient evidence and found no meaningful difference under the rubric. For A and C, both give day 30 and require a valid receipt. A reviewer can tie them if both are equally usable.
  • REVIEW means a winner or tie cannot be justified yet. If a reply says “first month” and no approved source gives that phrase a clear meaning, leave the comparison unresolved. A tie would imply the evidence had already supported equivalence.
Swap the displays and follow the stable IDs

Hide system names and use a recorded random assignment to choose the first display order across cases. This is blind randomization. Then show each selected pair in the opposite order in a separate judging pass. With two displays per pair, each candidate appears once in each slot. Preserve both records. Keep the question, policy, rubric, judge, and answer text fixed so you can inspect what changed.

Write the stable ID under each slot before you read a saved verdict. In the first display, slot A contains candidate A. After the swap, slot B contains that same answer. A judge that picks slot A first and slot B after the swap has followed the answer. A judge that picks slot A both times has followed the position in this replay, and its stable winner changes. Flag a tie that becomes a win as well. Keep REVIEW and malformed results visible. Under this lesson’s rule, two matching displays support one pair on one question. Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

For other presentation checks, hold the policy facts fixed. Put the same terms in a list or a paragraph to test formatting. Add “Certainly” without changing the facts to test confidence. Vary length separately from extra useful information. A result on one imagined pair tells you which comparison to inspect next. Repeat across several matched cases and saves before describing a preference as systematic.

Two judges can each be consistent under the swap and still prefer different answers. Keep their normalized outcomes separately. That is multi-model uncertainty when the judges are different models. Compare their cited evidence and ask a human reviewer to resolve important disagreements. Several judges can miss the same policy fact, so a majority still needs a factual check.

Count supported pairs and show the coverage

Start with one point for a win, half a point per candidate for a tie, and zero for a loss. This chapter uses these points as a simple summary. Take two wins and a tie. The points are 1 + 1 + 0.5 = 2.5, the win rate is 2/3, and the points per scored pair are 2.5/3. The two fractions answer different questions because the second gives partial credit for ties.

With four candidates, there are six possible unordered pairs. If you can score four of them, coverage is 4/6. Say which pairs were absent and which were attempted but unresolved. A candidate with two wins from three pairs can have more raw points than one with one win from one pair. Report both the pair counts and the points per pair. Normalizing helps expose unequal exposure. It cannot correct for different opponents, missing hard cases, or a player with no scored pairs. Report an unavailable rate for a zero denominator. Avoid treating a tied points total as a head-to-head tie.

Separate a summary from a defensible ranking

Draw an arrow from each winner to the loser. If A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A, the arrows form a cycle. A wins against B and loses to C, so no ordering puts every observed winner ahead of every loser. This pattern is called non-transitivity. Keep the cycle visible even if a points table has a top row. With incomplete comparisons, explain which extra pair would help before releasing a ranking.

A model such as Bradley–Terry tries to explain repeated decisive comparisons using one positive strength per candidate. If two fitted strengths were 2 and 1, the model would give the first candidate a win probability of 2 ÷ (2 + 1), about 0.67, for that matchup. The strengths come from a fit to many comparisons and need not equal raw points. The basic model handles wins and losses. Ties and abstentions need an explicitly chosen policy or extension. A single strength cannot reproduce all directions in a cycle, and disconnected groups lack evidence for a common ranking. Paired replays also share a question and need appropriate treatment as dependent observations. This chapter teaches the intuition and uses transparent points for its own report. Bradley and Terry, Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs

Keep the raw comparison ID, order, judge identity, question, frozen candidates, policy, rubric version, outcome, evidence, and reverse result. Record which results entered the aggregation, the ranking method, and all open review flags. A relative preference can put B above D even though B fails the critical refund gate. Keep that gate alongside the preference report before deciding which answers a customer can see.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. A plausible draft loses on the policy

User question. Can I get a refund for something I bought?

Approved reference. Harbor Leaf allows eligible requests through calendar day 30 after delivery. A valid receipt is required.

Actual LLM response. A says “Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” B says “Absolutely. You have 90 calendar days after delivery to request a refund, and a receipt is optional.”

Assessment. Check the starting event, date, and receipt first. A preserves all three. In B, “90 calendar days” contradicts the 30-day limit and “a receipt is optional” contradicts the requirement. A wins. The word “Absolutely” cannot change either fact. If you reviewed B pointwise, it would independently fail the refund-policy check.

Failure classification. Save A as the winner and record B’s two contradictions. The comparison supports a preference for this question. It gives no ranking of the systems on other refund questions.

Example 2. Follow the answer through the swap

User question. Can I get a refund for something I bought?

Approved reference. Use the same refund-1 policy and the pairwise-v1 rubric above in each display.

Actual LLM response. Compare the frozen A/B and B/C pairs. The fixture gives saved choices for two displays per pair.

Assessment. For A/B, order A,B selects slot A and order B,A selects slot B. Both normalize to candidate A. For B/C, order B,C selects slot B and order C,B also selects slot B. Those choices normalize to C and B respectively. The second pair changes winner when the slot changes, although no candidate text or policy changed.

Failure classification. Enter one win for A on A/B. Keep B/C out of the points table until a reviewer reads both displays and their reasons. In one display the judge rewards C for preserving the deadline. In the reverse it rewards B for sounding decisive. Ask the reviewer to put the two quoted deadlines next to the policy. The two fictional displays show where to investigate. A larger controlled replay would be needed to establish a persistent bias.

Example 3. Rank a complete table, then test a missing pair

User question. Which answer should be sent for this eligible refund question?

Approved reference. Use refund-1, and prefer the correct deadline and receipt condition before style.

Actual LLM response. Use the four frozen candidates. For this worked example, use independently resolved teaching outcomes for all six pairs. The raw audit in Step 7 is a different snapshot that retains open disagreements.

Assessment. Read the six results below. Give A 1 for each of two wins plus 0.5 for its tie. C also earns 2.5. D has one win and earns 1. B earns 0. Now remove B/C because its two displays disagree. C drops to 1.5 points across two scored pairs, and B has only two scored pairs. Coverage drops from 6/6 to 5/6. A’s 2.5 from three pairs and C’s 1.5 from two pairs come from different opponents.

Failure classification. Report A and C as tied by points in the complete snapshot. In the incomplete snapshot, report the difference as provisional and ask for B/C to be adjudicated. Confirm B independently fails policy, even if another replay ranks it above a generic referral.

Step 1 — Record a comparison and the reason

Store what was shown before interpreting the result. A dictionary maps names to values. The tuple "order" shows slot A first and slot B second. The nested candidate dictionary stores the texts by stable ID.

Slot A / ID A: Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Slot B / ID C: Bring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.
Recorded choice: TIE

Only the saved choice changes. In a real audit, keep the previous record and attach the evidence for a new verdict. Checkpoint. What would justify this tie? Both answers must be compared against the rubric with enough evidence to conclude that neither is meaningfully better.

Step 2 — Let a critical check take priority

Use a controlled variant of B that requires a valid receipt in both versions, so the deadline is the only policy fact whose value changes. The numbers and clarity ratings are reviewed inputs for the exercise. The Boolean result from == is true if the reviewed count matches 30. The if branches use the clarity preference only when both policy checks pass.

Open Python Editor

approved_days = 30
a_days = 30
b_days = 90
clarity_a, clarity_b = 3, 4
a_ok = a_days == approved_days
b_ok = b_days == approved_days
print(f"B says: Ask within {b_days} calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.")
print(f"Deadline check: A {a_ok} | B {b_ok}")
if a_ok != b_ok:
    winner = "A" if a_ok else "B"
elif not a_ok:
    winner = "REVIEW"
elif clarity_a == clarity_b:
    winner = "TIE"
else:
    winner = "A" if clarity_a > clarity_b else "B"
print(f"Fixture choice: {winner}")
Expected output
B says: Ask within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.
Deadline check: A True | B False
Fixture choice: A

Experiment. Change only b_days = 90 to b_days = 30.

Expected output
B says: Ask within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.
Deadline check: A True | B True
Fixture choice: B

With both deadline checks passing and the receipt held fixed, the clarity rating can decide the comparison. Checkpoint. Would this program catch a waiver of the receipt rule? The fixture assumed a valid receipt for both replies. Free-text answers still need evidence for the amount, unit, event, and receipt.

Step 3 — Normalize the two display choices

Map the first display slot to index 0 and the second to index 1. If the raw label is TIE or REVIEW, preserve it. Compare the two resulting values only after translating display labels to stable IDs.

Open Python Editor

def normalize(order, choice):
    if choice == "A":
        return order[0]
    if choice == "B":
        return order[1]
    return choice

first_order = ("B", "C")
reverse_order = ("C", "B")
first_choice = "B"
reverse_choice = "B"
first = normalize(first_order, first_choice)
reverse = normalize(reverse_order, reverse_choice)
print(f"Forward: slot {first_choice} -> ID {first}")
print(f"Reverse: slot {reverse_choice} -> ID {reverse}")
print("Supported pair" if first == reverse and first != "REVIEW" else "Send to review")
Expected output
Forward: slot B -> ID C
Reverse: slot B -> ID B
Send to review

Experiment. Change only reverse_choice from "B" to "A".

Expected output
Forward: slot B -> ID C
Reverse: slot A -> ID C
Supported pair

The reversed display now points to C as well. Checkpoint. How many supported pairs did the change produce? One. You used two displays of the same evidence to check sensitivity to order.

Step 4 — Count wins, losses, and ties

Use the complete resolved table from the worked demonstration. Count only rows involving A. The tuple stores both IDs and the winner, or TIE. continue skips a row involving neither slot. The win rate uses every scored appearance, including ties, in its denominator.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [("A", "B", "A"), ("A", "C", "TIE"), ("A", "D", "A"),
         ("B", "C", "C"), ("B", "D", "D"), ("C", "D", "C")]
wins = losses = ties = 0
for left, right, result in pairs:
    if "A" not in (left, right):
        continue
    if result == "TIE":
        ties += 1
    elif result == "A":
        wins += 1
    else:
        losses += 1

total = wins + losses + ties
points = wins + 0.5 * ties
print(f"A: {wins} wins | {losses} losses | {ties} ties | {total} scored")
print(f"Win rate: {100 * wins / total:.1f}%")
print(f"Points: {points:.1f} | points per pair: {points / total:.3f}")
Expected output
A: 2 wins | 0 losses | 1 ties | 3 scored
Win rate: 66.7%
Points: 2.5 | points per pair: 0.833

Experiment. Change the A/B result from "A" to "TIE".

Expected output
A: 1 wins | 0 losses | 2 ties | 3 scored
Win rate: 33.3%
Points: 2.0 | points per pair: 0.667

A loses one full win and gains a half-point tie. Three pairs still count. Checkpoint. If A/B instead needed REVIEW, should it count in the denominator? No. Keep the attempt in the audit and leave it out of the scored win rate.

Step 5 — Rank by points without breaking ties

Add one point for each winner and half a point per side for each tie. set(points.values()) keeps each distinct points total. sorted(..., reverse=True) visits those totals from highest to lowest. ' = '.join(...) displays every candidate in a tied group.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [("A", "B", "A"), ("A", "C", "TIE"), ("A", "D", "A"),
         ("B", "C", "C"), ("B", "D", "D"), ("C", "D", "C")]
points = {"A": 0.0, "B": 0.0, "C": 0.0, "D": 0.0}
for left, right, result in pairs:
    if result == "TIE":
        points[left] += 0.5
        points[right] += 0.5
    else:
        points[result] += 1

for score in sorted(set(points.values()), reverse=True):
    group = [name for name in points if points[name] == score]
    print(f"{' = '.join(group)}: {score:.1f} points")
Expected output
A = C: 2.5 points
D: 1.0 points
B: 0.0 points

Experiment. Change C/D’s result from "C" to "D".

Expected output
A: 2.5 points
D: 2.0 points
C: 1.5 points
B: 0.0 points

A keeps 2.5. One point moves from C to D. Checkpoint. Did the edited verdict prove D gives better policy advice? It changed the recorded points only. Inspect D’s generic referral and check the evidence before releasing it.

Step 6 — Find a cycle and show missing pairs

Represent a win as a tuple (winner, loser). combinations(ids, 2) gives each unordered pair once. tuple(sorted(edge)) puts both directions of a pair under the same key for coverage. For a three-way cycle, test the two directions starting at the earliest ID in each group of three. This small check detects three-candidate cycles.

Open Python Editor

from itertools import combinations

ids = ("A", "B", "C", "D")
edges = {("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")}
all_pairs = set(combinations(ids, 2))
scored = {tuple(sorted(edge)) for edge in edges}
cycles = []
for a, b, c in combinations(ids, 3):
    for x, y in ((b, c), (c, b)):
        if {(a, x), (x, y), (y, a)} <= edges:
            cycles.append(f"{a}>{x}>{y}>{a}")

missing = [a + b for a, b in sorted(all_pairs - scored)]
print(f"Scored pairs: {len(scored)}/{len(all_pairs)}")
print(f"Missing: {', '.join(missing)}")
print(f"Three-way cycles: {', '.join(cycles) or 'none'}")
Expected output
Scored pairs: 3/6
Missing: AD, BD, CD
Three-way cycles: A>B>C>A

Experiment. Remove only ("C", "A") from edges.

Expected output
Scored pairs: 2/6
Missing: AC, AD, BD, CD
Three-way cycles: none

Cross out the arrow from C to A. The two remaining arrows still say A beat B and B beat C, but you lost the direct comparison between A and C. Checkpoint. Which new result would bring the cycle back? A supported C win against A. Report the missing pair beside the cycle check so a reader can see what the program had enough evidence to find.

Step 7 — Build an auditable pairwise report

Replay all six unordered pairs. The first and reversed rows keep their display order, raw choice, and saved reason. These are stored examples of a balanced schedule, with one display in each order per pair. J1 is the primary fictional model judge. J2 is a different fictional model that supplies only a comparison on B/D. A reversal that changes the stable winner, or an abstention in either display, sends the pair to review. The baseline points summarize supported J1 results. It flags a stable J2 disagreement separately. A sensitivity check can withhold that pair from the table.

The program checks the reviewed policy facts separately. A confirmed wrong claim is FAIL, and missing facts need REVIEW. These values are supplied by a policy reader. The program neither interprets free text nor runs a judge. Its cycle check uses only decisive results included in the points table. It tries each possible path through a group of candidates once per starting ID. permutations() provides the possible orders after the first ID. path[1:] + path[:1] shifts the path by one step and wraps back to its start, so zip() pairs every stop with the next.

The dictionary audit preserves each pair and its two displays. The list rankable contains only candidates with a scored appearance. A missing reverse stays open. [::-1] reverses a tuple so the two orders can be checked before counting anything. A sorted set of their scores makes the report deterministic. Group equal points together and keep a total ranking provisional if coverage, cycles, or judge disagreements leave open questions.

Open Python Editor

from itertools import combinations, permutations

question = "Can I get a refund for something I bought?"
policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
policy_version = "refund-1"
rubric = "pairwise-v1"
aggregation = "primary"
# Frozen text, verified day count, and whether a valid receipt is required.
candidates = {
    "A": ("Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.", 30, True),
    "B": ("Absolutely. You have 90 calendar days after delivery to request a refund, and a receipt is optional.", 90, False),
    "C": ("Bring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.", 30, True),
    "D": ("Please contact customer support about refunds.", None, None),
}
# Each row keeps order, raw slot choice, and the saved judge's reason.
primary = {
    "AB": [(("A", "B"), "A", "chosen answer preserves the 30-day limit and receipt"),
           (("B", "A"), "B", "chosen answer preserves the 30-day limit and receipt")],
    "AC": [(("A", "C"), "TIE", "both preserve the required facts"),
           (("C", "A"), "TIE", "both preserve the required facts")],
    "AD": [(("A", "D"), "A", "chosen answer provides the deadline and receipt"),
           (("D", "A"), "B", "chosen answer provides the deadline and receipt")],
    "BC": [(("B", "C"), "B", "C preserves the 30-day limit"),
           (("C", "B"), "B", "B sounds decisive")],
    "BD": [(("B", "D"), "A", "B gives more detail"),
           (("D", "B"), "B", "B gives more detail")],
    "CD": [(("C", "D"), "REVIEW", "no supported comparison supplied"),
           (("D", "C"), "REVIEW", "no supported comparison supplied")],
}
secondary = {
    "BD": [(("B", "D"), "B", "D avoids giving the wrong deadline"),
           (("D", "B"), "A", "D avoids giving the wrong deadline")],
}

def normalize(order, choice):
    if choice in ("A", "B"):
        return order[0 if choice == "A" else 1]
    return choice if choice in ("TIE", "REVIEW") else "INVALID"

def supported(pair, views):
    if len(views) != 2:
        return "REVIEW", "missing reverse"
    first, reverse = views
    if set(first[0]) != set(pair) or reverse[0] != first[0][::-1]:
        return "REVIEW", "invalid display orders"
    outcomes = [normalize(order, choice) for order, choice, reason in views]
    if any(result in ("REVIEW", "INVALID") for result in outcomes):
        return "REVIEW", "abstention or invalid"
    if outcomes[0] != outcomes[1]:
        return "REVIEW", "order conflict"
    return outcomes[0], "supported"

def gate(days, receipt):
    if (days is not None and days != 30) or receipt is False:
        return "FAIL"
    if days is None or receipt is None:
        return "REVIEW"
    return "PASS"

ids = sorted(candidates)
counts = {name: dict(wins=0, losses=0, ties=0) for name in ids}
audit, edges, open_pairs, judge_disputes = {}, set(), [], []
scored = 0
print(f"{policy_version} | {rubric} | aggregation {aggregation}")
for a, b in combinations(ids, 2):
    pair = a + b
    views = primary.get(pair, [])
    result, reason = supported(pair, views)
    other_views = secondary.get(pair, [])
    other, _ = supported(pair, other_views)
    dispute = result != "REVIEW" and other != "REVIEW" and result != other
    if dispute:
        judge_disputes.append(pair)
    if dispute and aggregation == "exclude-disputes":
        result, reason = "REVIEW", "judge disagreement"
    audit[pair] = {
        "id": "P-" + pair, "question": question, "source": policy, "policy_version": policy_version,
        "rubric": rubric, "aggregation": aggregation, "stable_ids": (a, b),
        "candidate_texts": {name: candidates[name][0] for name in (a, b)},
        "J1_displays": views, "J2_displays": other_views, "judge_dispute": dispute,
        "table_result": result, "reason": reason,
    }
    choices = "/".join(normalize(order, choice) for order, choice, _ in views) or "none"
    print(f"P-{pair}: J1 {choices} | table {result} ({reason})")
    if result == "REVIEW":
        open_pairs.append(pair)
        continue
    scored += 1
    if result == "TIE":
        counts[a]["ties"] += 1
        counts[b]["ties"] += 1
    else:
        loser = b if result == a else a
        counts[result]["wins"] += 1
        counts[loser]["losses"] += 1
        edges.add((result, loser))

points, rankable, cycles = {}, [], []
for name, row in counts.items():
    wins, losses, ties = row["wins"], row["losses"], row["ties"]
    total = wins + losses + ties
    points[name] = wins + 0.5 * ties
    rate = f"{points[name] / total:.3f}" if total else "unavailable"
    if total:
        rankable.append(name)
    print(f"{name}: {wins}W {losses}L {ties}T | {points[name]:.1f} pts | {rate} per pair | policy {gate(*candidates[name][1:])}")

for length in range(3, len(ids) + 1):
    for group in combinations(ids, length):
        start = group[0]
        for tail in permutations(group[1:]):
            path = (start,) + tail
            next_nodes = path[1:] + path[:1]
            if set(zip(path, next_nodes)) <= edges:
                cycles.append(">".join(path + (start,)))
groups = ["=".join(name for name in rankable if points[name] == score)
          for score in sorted({points[name] for name in rankable}, reverse=True)]
attempted = sum(bool(entry["J1_displays"]) for entry in audit.values())
print(f"Attempted coverage: {attempted}/{len(audit)}")
print(f"Scored coverage: {scored}/{len(audit)} | open: {','.join(open_pairs) or 'none'}")
print(f"Cross-judge disputes: {','.join(judge_disputes) or 'none'}")
print(f"Cycles: {','.join(cycles) or 'none'}")
print("Points groups: " + (" > ".join(groups) or "unavailable"))
print("Total ranking: withheld" if open_pairs or judge_disputes or cycles else "Total ranking: points groups")
Expected output
refund-1 | pairwise-v1 | aggregation primary
P-AB: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-AC: J1 TIE/TIE | table TIE (supported)
P-AD: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-BC: J1 C/B | table REVIEW (order conflict)
P-BD: J1 B/B | table B (supported)
P-CD: J1 REVIEW/REVIEW | table REVIEW (abstention or invalid)
A: 2W 0L 1T | 2.5 pts | 0.833 per pair | policy PASS
B: 1W 1L 0T | 1.0 pts | 0.500 per pair | policy FAIL
C: 0W 0L 1T | 0.5 pts | 0.500 per pair | policy PASS
D: 0W 2L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy REVIEW
Attempted coverage: 6/6
Scored coverage: 4/6 | open: BC,CD
Cross-judge disputes: BD
Cycles: none
Points groups: A > B > C > D
Total ranking: withheld

Experiment. In the B/C reverse row, replace (("C", "B"), "B", "B sounds decisive") with (("C", "B"), "A", "C preserves the 30-day limit"). This is a replacement replay of one display. Save the earlier replay separately in a real audit.

Expected output
refund-1 | pairwise-v1 | aggregation primary
P-AB: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-AC: J1 TIE/TIE | table TIE (supported)
P-AD: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-BC: J1 C/C | table C (supported)
P-BD: J1 B/B | table B (supported)
P-CD: J1 REVIEW/REVIEW | table REVIEW (abstention or invalid)
A: 2W 0L 1T | 2.5 pts | 0.833 per pair | policy PASS
B: 1W 2L 0T | 1.0 pts | 0.333 per pair | policy FAIL
C: 1W 0L 1T | 1.5 pts | 0.750 per pair | policy PASS
D: 0W 2L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy REVIEW
Attempted coverage: 6/6
Scored coverage: 5/6 | open: CD
Cross-judge disputes: BD
Cycles: none
Points groups: A > C > B > D
Total ranking: withheld

The two displays now support C on B/C, adding one scored pair and a loss for B. A still has one more scored opponent than C. J1’s two stable B/D results are sufficient for this table under the primary rule. J2 picks D in both orders, so the report keeps their disagreement visible. Checkpoint. Would you release B because it won a supported pair? B independently fails on the deadline and receipt. Inspect the saved reasons for B/D, get another review of C/D, and keep the points groups provisional.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Apply the policy-first rubric

Compare A with B using refund-1. Then compare A with C. Decide when you have a supported winner and when a tie is justified. Name the evidence for each result.

Practice 2. Read the reversed display

The first display puts C in slot A and D in slot B. The judge chooses A. The second display puts D in slot A and C in slot B. The judge chooses A again. Translate both choices and decide what goes in the scored table.

Practice 3. Calculate points when two candidates tie

In the complete resolved snapshot, A halves its A/C pair with C and beats B and D. C beats B and D. D beats B. Calculate each points total and the points-per-pair of the two leaders. Do the totals establish a unique winner?

Practice 4. Read a cycle with missing evidence

In a small replay, A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. D has no comparisons. Compute coverage over all four candidates and identify which claims would be defensible in an audit. What should the team compare next?

Independent Assignment

Use the full Step 7 program as the standalone answer key. First read the four frozen answers and record each policy status using refund-1. Normalize every display. List which pairs came from repeated displays of the same evidence, which are open, and where the two judges disagree. Verify the table counts, coverage, and points groups by hand. Write a release recommendation supported by the critical facts as well as the preferences.

For variant A, start from the Step 7 experiment, where B/C consistently supports C. Replace the two C/D rows with (("C", "D"), "B", "D gives an escalation path") and (("D", "C"), "A", "D gives an escalation path"). The revised replay prefers D in both orders. For variant B, start from the baseline and change only aggregation = "primary" to aggregation = "exclude-disputes". Keep all text, evidence, and display choices fixed. In both variants save a review recommendation and explain when the ranked points fail to settle it.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

A wins A/B. Both replies count from delivery, but B says 90 instead of 30 and makes the receipt optional. These two contradictions outweigh B’s confident wording. A and C both give the 30-day rule and require a valid receipt. If both are similarly clear for the customer, record TIE. An ambiguous “first month” version of C would need clarification before deciding whether it satisfies the same cutoff.

Solution 2

The first displayed A means candidate C. The reversed displayed A means candidate D. The stable winner changes from C to D. Log both raw outcomes and leave the pair unresolved. Inspect whether the judge anchored on the first slot or had another reason before asking for adjudication.

Solution 3

A and C each earn 1 + 1 + 0.5 = 2.5 over three pairs, or 0.833 points per pair. D has one win and two losses, so it earns 1. B loses every pair and earns 0. The two leaders are tied by points. This fixture also records a supported head-to-head tie between them. Another dataset can give equal totals even without a head-to-head tie.

Solution 4

List all six pairs first: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD. Three contain a scored result, giving 50% coverage. Try putting A first. The C-over-A result immediately conflicts with that choice. Starting with B or C has the same problem. D has no scored comparison, so its rate is unavailable. Ask for both display orders on A/D, B/D, and C/D. Review the three existing reasons before proposing an order for all four.

Assignment answer key

The baseline has 4/6 coverage, with B/C and C/D in review. A and C pass the policy, B fails it, and D lacks the facts. B/D is supported by J1 in both orders. J2 points to D both times. Keep both records. The policy failure means the team should hold B even if a scoring method raises it above D.

For variant A, the changed lines from the Step 7 experiment are P-CD: J1 D/D | table D (supported), C: 1W 1L 1T | 1.5 pts | 0.500 per pair | policy PASS, D: 1W 2L 0T | 1.0 pts | 0.333 per pair | policy REVIEW, Scored coverage: 6/6 | open: none, Cycles: B>D>C>B, and Points groups: A > C > B=D. Keep every other line. Ask a reviewer to inspect the three edges in the cycle and the raw B/D disagreement. Complete coverage does not make these preferences transitive.

For variant B, the changed lines from the baseline are refund-1 | pairwise-v1 | aggregation exclude-disputes, P-BD: J1 B/B | table REVIEW (judge disagreement), B: 0W 1L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy FAIL, D: 0W 1L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy REVIEW, Scored coverage: 3/6 | open: BC,BD,CD, and Points groups: A > C > B=D. The disagreement is still listed, and the total ranking is withheld. Reducing coverage exposes how much the baseline placement depended on one disputed win.

Knowledge Check

  1. A reply beats a vague referral but tells the customer the receipt is optional. Which separate evaluation answers whether it can be sent?
  2. Both replies satisfy the rules and one is shorter. When should conciseness influence the result?
  3. The policy page is missing and the judge cannot check either deadline. Which output should it return and why?
  4. Why start from a blind randomized display order and collect the reverse as well?
  5. Stable A is in slot B and wins. In the swapped display it is in slot A and wins. How many supported pair outcomes go into the table?
  6. A candidate wins twice, ties once, and loses once. Give its wins-per-scored-pair and points-per-scored-pair.
  7. A points summary puts a candidate first even though its preference arrows form a cycle. What should the audit say?
  8. Two model judges each agree with their own reversed replay but disagree with one another. What evidence is needed before deciding which answer to send?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Apply a pointwise policy check to that reply. It fails because refund-1 requires a valid receipt, regardless of its relative preference.
  2. Check completeness and clarity first. If both are adequate and the shorter wording is easier to use without losing a needed detail, use the conciseness criterion. A small difference can still justify a tie.
  3. Return REVIEW. A tie needs evidence that the compared answers are equivalent under the rubric.
  4. Blinding reduces influence from knowing the source system. Randomization spreads initial slot placement, and the reverse exposes choices that change when the stable texts swap slots.
  5. One. Both display choices normalize to the same stable answer on a single pair.
  6. The win rate is 2/4, or 50%. The points are 2 + 0.5 = 2.5, so the points rate is 2.5/4 = 0.625.
  7. Show the cycle alongside the points and report that the ordering cannot satisfy every observed preference. Include coverage and review the conflicting comparisons.
  8. Inspect both reasons, the original question, the exact responses, and the source. Apply the independent critical checks and ask a human reviewer to adjudicate the disputed comparison.

Common Mistakes

Map each display label back to the stable answer before comparing the outcomes. A raw slot label can point to a different answer after a swap.

Track ties, unresolved attempts, absent pairs, and cross-judge disputes separately. These outcomes change the evidence available to a ranking.

Always check each answer against the approved policy before release. Ranking points summarize relative choices on the collected pairs.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

A pairwise comparison answers which of two frozen responses serves the customer better under a stated rule. Keep stable IDs and normalize reversed display choices. Report counts, coverage, cycles, and open disputes alongside any points groups. An independent check is needed for the facts a customer will act on.

Next, Variance, repetition and score aggregation examines what repeated evaluations tell you about variation and how to combine results across cases.

Intermediate · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Design controlled repeats and identify whether the response, judge, case set, or effective settings changed.
  • Calculate mean, median, range, population variance, and standard deviation from saved scores.
  • Separate variation within one case from differences between cases, and explain why repeated draws do not add distinct cases.
  • Calculate per-run, per-case, and pooled summaries. Show how slice weights, missing rows, and policy failures affect the interpretation.
  • Reproduce a report from its saved inputs and state what further evidence a decision needs.

Why This Lesson Matters

The first time Harbor Leaf Market tests its refund assistant, nine out of ten judged answers pass. Someone puts 90% in the release notes. Then the next two runs return 70% and 80%. Before the team edits the headline, it needs to find out whether the assistant gave different answers, the judge rated the same answers differently, or a different set of questions was counted.

The examples are fictional. Harbor Leaf keeps the policy used in the earlier lessons, refund-1: “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included for eligible unused online purchases. The opening numbers are run-level pass percentages. Later, the audit uses presentation scores on a 0–100 scale and a separate policy check.

Allow about 5.5 hours. Start with Objectives, dimensions and failure taxonomy. Inference, sampling and repeatability, Sampling, holdouts, leakage and maintenance, and Combining evaluators and handling uncertainty are useful refreshers.

Beginner Explanation

Find what changed before repeating

Read the 90%, 70%, and 80% alongside their run logs. First identify what was measured. If a run answered ten questions, 90% can mean nine passed judgments out of ten valid binary results. Check the counts and the criteria before comparing that score with another percentage.

  • To investigate assistant variation, ask the same questions again under the same generation procedure. Keep the judge and scoring rule fixed. Save each answer so you can see which wording changed.
  • To investigate judge variation, replay the exact same frozen answers against the same rubric and judge configuration. Compare the individual verdicts on each answer.
  • To investigate the effect of the questions sampled, freeze the settings and document which case IDs were selected. A set with more deadline questions can score differently even without a change to the assistant or judge.
  • To evaluate a configuration change, choose which factor to change and record both versions. A different rubric, judge, or aggregation rule can move the score even when every reply stays fixed.

A seed is a value used to initialize a random procedure. Record it, or the planned seed sequence, along with the model version, prompt, sampling settings, and scoring versions. The effective configuration is what actually ran, including resolved defaults. Check whether a requested setting was applied. Preserve the dataset and generation procedure or exact response records, judge, rubric, aggregation, and run ID. A seed can help reproduce a sampling procedure without guaranteeing that a live service produces the same result.

If the evaluation uses a service that loads work lazily, record whether each run started cold, before a first request warmed it, or warm, after a documented warm-up. Compare like starts when measuring latency. A timeout can also change which scores enter a quality mean. Record it before trying to explain a change in the mean.

Running the same arithmetic twice is a deterministic repeat. Replaying saved judge outcomes verifies the report and the decisions that follow from those outcomes. Generating fresh live replies or asking a live judge to score again measures another source of variation. The Python in this lesson replays invented data.

Read the observed scores before summarizing

Suppose two more runs return 80% and 80%. The five scores are 70, 80, 90, 80, 80. Put them on a number line and place one mark at 70, three at 80, and one at 90. This pattern of observed scores is their distribution.

Add the five values to get 400. Divide by the five runs to get 80. This arithmetic mean describes the center of the observed scores. It leaves the spread out of view.

Sort the scores to get 70, 80, 80, 80, 90. The middle score is 80, the median. With an even number of scores, average the middle two. If the 90 were instead a 20, the sum would fall to 330 and the mean to 66. The middle score would still be 80. Inspect the 20. It could be a real failure or a run with a configuration change.

The minimum is 70 and the maximum is 90. Their difference is 20 percentage points, the range. It shows the distance between the observed extremes. It does not tell how many runs were near either end.

Measure distance from the mean

Put 70 and 90 on either side of the mean, 80. They are both ten points from the center. If you subtract 80 from each of the scores 70, 80, 90, you get −10, 0, 10. Adding those differences would give zero and hide both ten-point gaps. Square each difference and the two gaps both contribute 100. The middle score contributes zero. The total is 200.

Divide 200 by all three observed runs to get 66.67, the population variance of these three saved scores. Its units are squared percentage points because the distances were squared. Take the square root to get population standard deviation, about 8.16 percentage points. It summarizes observed spread in the same units as the scores. It gives no guaranteed bound on a future run.

If you wanted to estimate a wider population’s variance from a suitable sample under the usual assumptions, the standard sample variance calculation would divide by one less than the number of observations. For these three, it would give 100. This lesson uses population variance throughout to describe the complete lists on screen. Repeated scores from the same case do not automatically satisfy the independence assumptions for inference.

Choose what counts as one observation

If you read Q1 twice and Q2 twice, you have four recorded observations and two distinct questions. An analysis unit is what you count as one observation for a particular statement. Use the case to report question coverage. Use a repeated attempt within that case to describe how its scores changed.

Here is a small case-by-setting plot. Each cell uses the same 50–100 scale. Read left to right, with each character advancing two points. An asterisk marks each observed score. The exact scores are printed beside the marks. The numbers are presentation scores. Both settings saw the same case IDs and a fixed rubric.

Course hours by track
Case and sliceSetting X, two observationsSetting Y, two observations
R, routine......................*.*. 94, 98....................*.*... 90, 94
H, deadline....*.*................... 58, 62...........*.*............ 72, 76

Within-case variation is the spread of repeats on the same question and setting. For X on R, the scores differ by four points. For X, the case means are 96 and 60. Their difference shows between-case variation, the change in the center from one question to another. Here is the variance version of the same comparison. Within either X case the two distances from its mean are −2 and 2, giving population variance (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4. Compare the two case means, 96 and 60, around their own center of 78. Their population variance is (324 + 324) ÷ 2 = 324. Keep the unit next to each result. Repeats on R share whatever makes R easy or hard, so four observations across R and H still give you only two distinct questions.

A slice is a group of questions that share a trait. With equal weight on routine and deadline, X scores (96 + 60) ÷ 2 = 78 and Y scores (92 + 74) ÷ 2 = 83. Now give routine 90% of the weight and deadline 10%, using the same weights for both settings. X scores 0.90 × 96 + 0.10 × 60 = 92.4. Y scores 0.90 × 92 + 0.10 × 74 = 90.2. The order reverses even though every saved score stays fixed. Choose and document slice weights before comparing. These two weighting plans answer different questions.

Choose an aggregation and show its denominator

To summarize one case across runs, average its eligible repeat scores. To summarize one run across cases, average its eligible scores across the cases in that run. An equal-run mean gives every run the same weight, even when one run scored fewer rows. This is a macro mean over runs. A pooled micro mean gives every valid, scorable row the same weight. Weighting each run mean by its number of scored rows reproduces the micro result. An equal-case macro mean is another option if each distinct case should contribute equally.

A missing result can come from a skipped case or a timeout. If failures are more likely on deadline questions, excluding those rows can make a mean look better by changing the case mix. An invalid result might be unreadable. A valid abstention is readable and says no numeric judgment was made. Set these aside with reasons rather than filling in zero. In the audit report below, attempted / planned includes timeouts, valid / attempted counts usable verdict records including abstentions, and scorable / valid counts numeric verdicts. Also show scorable / planned as end-to-end coverage. Keep denominators visible and use “unavailable” when there is nothing to divide by.

A critical policy failure remains a failure even if its presentation score is high or missing. Count it separately and keep its case ID. A consistent presentation score can be useful if predictable wording matters. Stable bad advice still needs to be fixed. A small set of repeats helps find cases to inspect. It cannot establish live reliability or justify a precise confidence claim.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Replace a headline with the observed spread

User question. What should the team conclude after the first 90% refund-policy test?

Approved reference. Use the same refund-1 cases and pass rule for the saved repeats.

Actual LLM response. The fictional batch of five runs yields 90%, 70%, 80%, 80%, and 80%.

Assessment. The total is 400 and there are five results, so the mean is 80%. Sort them to see that the median is also 80%. The lowest and highest are 70% and 90%, giving a range of 20 percentage points.

Failure classification. Treat 90% as one observed result. Review the 70% run by case ID, and compare the effective configuration and scorable counts before attributing the difference to generation or judging.

Example 2. Compare runs with the same center

User question. Which setting gives more predictable presentation scores in these saved runs?

Approved reference. The rubric, judge and refund questions are fixed for this toy comparison. Policy is verified separately.

Actual LLM response. The saved scores are 78, 80, 82 for the steadier setting and 70, 80, 90 for the wider setting.

Assessment. Both means are 80. The first series has distances −2, 0 and 2. The squared distances total 8, so population variance is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and standard deviation is about 1.63. The second series has squared distances totaling 200. Population variance is 200/3 ≈ 66.67 and standard deviation is about 8.16.

Failure classification. The first setting varied less in these runs. Open the 70-point run for the second setting and look for the cases that pulled it down. Then open the policy checks for the steadier setting too. If it repeatedly tells customers they get 90 days, its consistent presentation is no reason to release it.

Example 3. Count what each average leaves out

User question. Has setting X produced enough evidence to release the refund assistant?

Approved reference. A request for an eligible item must be made through calendar day 30 after delivery and with a valid receipt. Presentation scores measure how the advice is communicated.

Actual LLM response. In X1, Q1 earns 90, Q2 earns 70, and Q3 earns 90 while promising a 90-day deadline. Q4 is skipped. In X2, Q1 earns 100, Q2 returns an invalid verdict, Q3 has a valid abstention, and Q4 times out.

Assessment. X1’s mean is 250/3 ≈ 83.33 and X2’s is 100/1 = 100. Equal run weight gives 91.67. Pooling the scored rows gives (250 + 100) ÷ (3 + 1) = 87.50. Report 7/8 attempted, 5/7 valid, 4/5 scorable, and 4/8 scorable end to end. The 90-day reply still fails the policy even though its presentation scored 90.

Failure classification. Block release on the verified critical violation. Inspect the invalid verdict and timeout, and repeat only after identifying the failed stage. If the question is how results change with a different case mix, test declared slice weights on fixed cases, as in the case-by-setting plot above. Do not compare the averages without their denominators.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Choose Copy Code, open the editor next to the activity, paste the entire program, and select Run. Compare the output before making the one described change. Start each step in a fresh editor. All programs use standard Python and inline fictional records. None runs a live model or judge.

Step 1 — Record the first three runs

Keep the run IDs next to the percentages so you can trace an unusual result. Each tuple groups an ID and a score. The for loop assigns each pair’s values to run_id and score. An f"..." string places those values where you see braces.

Open Python Editor

runs = [("R1", 90), ("R2", 70), ("R3", 80)]
for run_id, score in runs:
    print(f"{run_id}: {score}%")
print(f"Recorded runs: {len(runs)}")
Expected output
R1: 90%
R2: 70%
R3: 80%
Recorded runs: 3

Experiment. Add ("R4", 60) at the end of runs.

Expected output
R1: 90%
R2: 70%
R3: 80%
R4: 60%
Recorded runs: 4

The fourth run adds a lower observed value and leaves the earlier values intact. Checkpoint. What would you inspect before deciding R4 was worse? Check case IDs, raw verdicts, coverage, and versions. A changed result is a starting point for investigation.

Step 2 — See what an extreme value changes

The first five percentages cluster around 80. Import mean and median from Python’s statistics module. These functions return the arithmetic average and the middle of the sorted values. :.1f prints one decimal place.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, median

scores = [70, 80, 90, 80, 80]
print(f"Sorted: {sorted(scores)}")
print(f"Mean: {mean(scores):.1f}")
print(f"Median: {median(scores):.1f}")
Expected output
Sorted: [70, 80, 80, 80, 90]
Mean: 80.0
Median: 80.0

Experiment. Replace only the 90 in scores with 20.

Expected output
Sorted: [20, 70, 80, 80, 80]
Mean: 66.0
Median: 80.0

The sum lost 70 points, so the mean fell by 70/5 = 14. The middle position still holds 80. Checkpoint. Would you discard the 20 because the median stayed at 80? Keep it and trace the run. The median and the unusual value each tell you something the other misses.

Step 3 — Measure spread around a fixed mean

Construct three run percentages around 80. The variable offset sets how far the two outside scores are from the middle. min() and max() find the extremes. The p in pvariance() and pstdev() denotes population. These functions describe the complete three-value list using division by three before the square root.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, pvariance, pstdev

center = 80
offset = 2
scores = [center - offset, center, center + offset]
print(f"Scores: {scores} | mean {mean(scores):.2f}")
print(f"Min {min(scores)} | max {max(scores)} | range {max(scores) - min(scores)}")
print(f"Population variance: {pvariance(scores):.2f}")
print(f"Population SD: {pstdev(scores):.2f}")
Expected output
Scores: [78, 80, 82] | mean 80.00
Min 78 | max 82 | range 4
Population variance: 2.67
Population SD: 1.63

Experiment. Change offset = 2 to offset = 10.

Expected output
Scores: [70, 80, 90] | mean 80.00
Min 70 | max 90 | range 20
Population variance: 66.67
Population SD: 8.16

The center stayed fixed and the squared distances rose from 8 in total to 200. Checkpoint. What would using the sample formula change? It would divide 200 by 2 and give 100. Label the variance convention so readers can reproduce the result.

Step 4 — Compare average and stability separately

Compare the earlier two example settings. A dictionary groups the repeated scores under their setting IDs. items() gives each ID with its list. Report mean and population standard deviation together.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, pstdev

scores = {"X": [78, 80, 82], "Y": [70, 80, 90]}
for name, runs in scores.items():
    print(f"{name}: mean {mean(runs):.2f} | population SD {pstdev(runs):.2f}")
Expected output
X: mean 80.00 | population SD 1.63
Y: mean 80.00 | population SD 8.16

Experiment. Replace X’s last score, 82, with 88.

Expected output
X: mean 82.00 | population SD 4.32
Y: mean 80.00 | population SD 8.16

X’s center increased, while the new score also spread its values further apart. Checkpoint. Which setting had the smaller observed spread after the edit? X. Check the policy results and compare more matched cases before treating this score summary as a release decision.

Step 5 — Give runs or scored rows equal weight

Start with two presentation scores for each of two runs. The dictionary under a run ID stores case IDs and scores. set().union(*runs.values()) collects distinct case IDs from all nested dictionaries. sorted() gives them a stable output order. The list expression after values = collects a case’s score from every run that has one.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean

runs = {"R1": {"Q1": 90, "Q2": 70}, "R2": {"Q1": 100, "Q2": 80}}
case_ids = sorted(set().union(*runs.values()))
for name in case_ids:
    values = [run[name] for run in runs.values() if name in run]
    print(f"{name}: mean {mean(values):.2f} ({len(values)} scored)")

run_means, pooled = [], []
for run_id, run in runs.items():
    run_means.append(mean(run.values()))
    pooled.extend(run.values())
    print(f"{run_id}: mean {run_means[-1]:.2f} ({len(run)} scored)")
print(f"Equal-run mean: {mean(run_means):.2f}")
print(f"Pooled score mean: {mean(pooled):.2f}")
Expected output
Q1: mean 95.00 (2 scored)
Q2: mean 75.00 (2 scored)
R1: mean 80.00 (2 scored)
R2: mean 90.00 (2 scored)
Equal-run mean: 85.00
Pooled score mean: 85.00

Experiment. Add "Q3": 100 only inside R2’s dictionary.

Expected output
Q1: mean 95.00 (2 scored)
Q2: mean 75.00 (2 scored)
Q3: mean 100.00 (1 scored)
R1: mean 80.00 (2 scored)
R2: mean 93.33 (3 scored)
Equal-run mean: 86.67
Pooled score mean: 88.00

Draw five boxes for the scores after the edit. Two belong to R1 and three to R2. A pooled mean gives each box one vote, so R2 gets three votes. An equal-run mean gives each run one vote. Checkpoint. Which case has only one score behind its mean? Q3. Say so in the report, especially if someone wants to compare its mean with Q1 or Q2, where each was scored twice.

Step 6 — Keep missing, invalid, and abstained results visible

Four cases were planned. None means no usable response arrived. "ABSTAIN" is a valid verdict with no numeric rating. type(raw) is int prevents a true/false flag from being counted as a numeric score. 0 <= raw <= 100 tests both bounds.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean

rows = {"Q1": 90, "Q2": "bad", "Q3": None, "Q4": "ABSTAIN"}
scores = []
missing = invalid = abstained = 0
for raw in rows.values():
    if raw is None:
        missing += 1
    elif raw == "ABSTAIN":
        abstained += 1
    elif type(raw) is int and 0 <= raw <= 100:
        scores.append(raw)
    else:
        invalid += 1
print(f"Valid: {len(scores) + abstained} | missing: {missing} | invalid: {invalid}")
print(f"Abstentions: {abstained} | scorable coverage: {len(scores)}/{len(rows)}")
print(f"Valid numeric mean: {mean(scores):.2f}" if scores else "Valid numeric mean: unavailable")
Expected output
Valid: 2 | missing: 1 | invalid: 1
Abstentions: 1 | scorable coverage: 1/4
Valid numeric mean: 90.00

Experiment. Replace Q2’s "bad" with the number 70.

Expected output
Valid: 3 | missing: 1 | invalid: 0
Abstentions: 1 | scorable coverage: 2/4
Valid numeric mean: 80.00

A previously excluded case is now scorable. Coverage rises and the mean falls because the new 70 is below 90. Checkpoint. Did Q1 get worse? Its score stayed at 90. Trace the lower mean to newly available evidence before crediting or blaming a change in the assistant.

Step 7 — Reproduce a score report and its release decision

Compare two fictional sampling settings on the same four planned questions and the same presentation rubric. The reply records include wording and a separate policy decision supplied by a human reviewer. A row is a planned run–case pair. The report saves the case, reply ID and text, original and replayed verdict values, effective settings, policy result, and action. A policy failure takes priority over an unscorable verdict. Keep all observed rows and the score filters so another evaluator can reconstruct the report.

observed holds the historical fixture. The changes dictionary describes independent replay variants. Looking up a replacement with .get() leaves the historical rows intact. Check the original raw value beside the replayed value in the audit. For the spread of both per-run means and pooled scores we use population standard deviation, using all the saved values in the corresponding list.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, median, pvariance, pstdev

policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
dataset = "refund-eval-1"
rubric = "presentation-v1"
judge = "fictional-judge-r1 | temperature 0"
judge_replay = "saved-verdicts-1"
revision = "baseline"
questions = {
    "Q1": "What is the refund deadline?",
    "Q2": "Do I need a receipt for an eligible refund?",
    "Q3": "Can I still request a refund 45 days after delivery?",
    "Q4": "Can I ask for a refund on day 30 with my receipt?",
}
# Text and independently reviewed policy result.
replies = {
    "deadline": ("Ask through calendar day 30 after delivery.", "PASS"),
    "receipt": ("You need a valid receipt.", "PASS"),
    "wrong": ("You can still request a refund. You have 90 days after delivery with a valid receipt.", "FAIL"),
    "expired": ("Day 45 is outside the 30-calendar-day refund window after delivery.", "PASS"),
    "boundary": ("Yes. Day 30 after delivery is included, with a valid receipt.", "PASS"),
}
generation = {"X": "refund-assistant-r1 | temperature 0.7", "Y": "refund-assistant-r1 | temperature 0.2"}
# Setting, generation seed, start state. These are saved, effective fixture values.
runs = {
    "X1": ("X", 41, "warm"), "X2": ("X", 42, "warm"),
    "Y1": ("Y", 41, "warm"), "Y2": ("Y", 42, "warm"),
}
# Captured reply ID, attempt flag, raw result. An absent row was never attempted.
observed = {
    "X1": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 90), "Q2": ("receipt", True, 70), "Q3": ("wrong", True, 90)},
    "X2": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 100), "Q2": ("receipt", True, "bad"), "Q3": ("expired", True, "ABSTAIN"),
           "Q4": (None, True, None)},
    "Y1": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 88), "Q2": ("receipt", True, 76), "Q3": ("expired", True, 84),
           "Q4": ("boundary", True, 82)},
    "Y2": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 90), "Q2": ("receipt", True, 78), "Q3": ("expired", True, 80),
           "Q4": ("boundary", True, 82)},
}
changes = {"baseline": {}, "rescore": {("X1", "Q3"): 60},
           "repair": {("X2", "Q2"): 80}, "abstain": {("Y2", "Q4"): "ABSTAIN"}}

def status(attempted, reply, raw):
    if not attempted:
        return "SKIPPED"
    if reply is None:
        return "TIMEOUT"
    if raw == "ABSTAIN":
        return "ABSTAIN"
    if type(raw) is int and 0 <= raw <= 100:
        return "SCORED"
    return "INVALID"

def fraction(count, total):
    return f"{count}/{total}" if total else "unavailable"

audit = []
for run, (setting, seed, start) in runs.items():
    for case, question in questions.items():
        reply, attempted, original = observed[run].get(case, (None, False, None))
        raw = changes[revision].get((run, case), original)
        text, gate = replies.get(reply, (None, "UNKNOWN"))
        validity = status(attempted, reply, raw)
        action = "BLOCK" if gate == "FAIL" else ("REVIEW" if validity != "SCORED" or gate == "UNKNOWN" else "CHECKED")
        audit.append({
            "run": run, "setting": setting, "dataset": dataset, "policy": policy,
            "policy_version": "refund-1", "generation": generation[setting],
            "seed": seed, "start": start, "rubric": rubric, "judge": judge, "judge_replay": judge_replay,
            "case": case, "question": question, "reply": reply, "text": text,
            "attempted": attempted, "original": original, "raw": raw,
            "status": validity, "gate": gate, "review": action, "revision": revision,
            "aggregation": "pooled scorable rows and equal-run mean",
        })

print(f"{dataset} | {rubric} | {judge_replay} | revision {revision}")
for setting, effective in generation.items():
    print(f"Setting {setting}: {effective}")
    rows = [row for row in audit if row["setting"] == setting]
    scores = [row["raw"] for row in rows if row["status"] == "SCORED"]
    run_means = []
    for run in runs:
        if runs[run][0] != setting:
            continue
        values = [row["raw"] for row in rows if row["run"] == run and row["status"] == "SCORED"]
        average = f"{mean(values):.2f}" if values else "unavailable"
        print(f"  {run}: {average} ({len(values)} scored)")
        if values:
            run_means.append(mean(values))

    attempted = sum(row["attempted"] for row in rows)
    valid = sum(row["status"] in ("SCORED", "ABSTAIN") for row in rows)
    print(f"  attempted {fraction(attempted, len(rows))} | valid {fraction(valid, attempted)} | "
          f"scorable {fraction(len(scores), valid)} | end-to-end {fraction(len(scores), len(rows))}")
    if scores:
        print(f"  micro mean {mean(scores):.2f} | median {median(scores):.2f} | "
              f"min {min(scores)} | max {max(scores)} | range {max(scores) - min(scores)}")
        print(f"  row population variance {pvariance(scores):.2f} | row population SD {pstdev(scores):.2f}")
        print(f"  macro run mean {mean(run_means):.2f} | run-mean population SD {pstdev(run_means):.2f}")
    else:
        print("  score summaries unavailable")

    gaps = [f"{row['run']}/{row['case']}:{row['status']}" for row in rows if row["status"] != "SCORED"]
    failures = [f"{row['run']}/{row['case']}" for row in rows if row["gate"] == "FAIL"]
    print("  gaps " + (", ".join(gaps) or "none"))
    print("  critical " + (", ".join(failures) or "none observed"))
    needs_review = any(row["review"] == "REVIEW" for row in rows)
    decision = "BLOCK" if failures else ("REVIEW" if needs_review else "CONTINUE EVALUATION")
    print(f"  decision {decision}")

sample = next(row for row in audit if (row["run"], row["case"]) == ("X1", "Q3"))
print(f"Audit X1/Q3: {sample['reply']} | original {sample['original']} | "
      f"replay {sample['raw']} | policy {sample['gate']} | decision {sample['review']}")
Expected output
