The new presentation judgment lowers X’s mean and increases its observed spread. Its release decision stays BLOCK because the candidate still contradicts the policy. Checkpoint. How can Y have zero spread across its run means and nonzero spread across its rows? Different case scores can sum to the same total. State the unit before interpreting stability. Compare the settings on more matched scorable cases before attributing a difference to temperature.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Calculate the center of three repeats

Three fictional pass rates are 90%, 70%, and 80%. Calculate their mean. Explain what evidence you would inspect before attributing the 70% result to the assistant.

Practice 2. Calculate range and population standard deviation

Three presentation scores are 74, 80, and 86. Find the mean, range, variance, and standard deviation using all three observed values. Explain the units of the last two results.

Practice 3. Compare steadiness and average quality

Setting X has scores 78, 80, 82. Setting Y has scores 70, 80, 90. Show the mean and population standard deviation for each. Suppose the reviewer finds a critical failure in X and none in these three Y scores. Explain what can be concluded and what evidence is still needed.

Practice 4. Audit a missing-heavy average

X1 has three scorable rows, 90, 70, 90, one skipped case, and a critical failure on the last scored row. X2 has 100, one invalid verdict, one valid abstention, and one timeout. Each run planned four rows. Calculate equal-run and pooled means, all four coverage ratios, and the release decision. Name the minimum facts someone would need to reproduce the report.

Independent Assignment

You are reviewing the four saved runs and four questions in Step 7. First write down the dataset, rubric, judge replay, effective generation settings, and the independent policy rule. Recalculate each run mean and compare pooled means and medians, ranges, population variances, and population standard deviations for X and Y. Explain why neither repeated attempts nor matching seed values make the individual rows independent questions. Use the audit record to show which critical case blocks release. Give a plan for investigating each kind of missing score.

Use the complete Step 7 program as the executable answer key. Select Copy Code and start from a fresh copy for each variant. For variant A set revision = "repair" to replay a valid 80 for X2/Q2. For variant B instead set revision = "abstain" to replay a valid abstention on Y2/Q4. Each replay keeps the original response and historical raw score. Report which coverage ratio and spread change, whether policy evidence changes, and whether to block, review, or continue evaluating. Finish by explaining why the same weights and comparable case coverage matter if someone wants to use these configurations for a comparative decision.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Add 90 + 70 + 80 = 240. Divide by three to get 80%. Open the 70% run and check the case IDs, saved replies, and verdicts. Verify the effective generation and judge settings, rubric, and scorable counts before interpreting the drop.

Solution 2

The mean is (74 + 80 + 86) ÷ 3 = 80. Range is 86 − 74 = 12 points. Deviations are −6, 0, and 6. Their squares sum to 36 + 0 + 36 = 72. Population variance is 72 ÷ 3 = 24 squared points. Standard deviation is √24 ≈ 4.90 points.

Solution 3

Both means are 80. X has squared deviations totaling 8, giving population variance 8/3 and standard deviation 1.63. Y has squared deviations totaling 200, giving population variance 200/3 and standard deviation 8.16. X is steadier on these scores and still fails the policy gate. Investigate that failure before release. Check more matched cases and separate sources of variation before making a claim about either setting’s live reliability.

Solution 4

Give X1 and X2 one vote each and you get (250/3 + 100) ÷ 2, about 91.67. Give the four scored rows one vote each and you get 350 ÷ 4 = 87.50. Now account for the other rows. Seven of eight were attempted, including the timeout. Five of those seven produced a valid record, and four of those five gave a number. So end-to-end coverage is 4/8. Block the 90-day reply using the policy evidence. Save the case and run IDs, raw outcomes, effective settings, policy decisions, versions, and weighting rule so another reviewer can reconstruct both averages and the block.

Assignment answer key

X has the higher baseline pooled presentation mean and greater row spread, but only four of eight planned rows contribute scores. Y’s two run means match, and its rows still vary. Review X’s missing or unusable evidence and block its verified 90-day reply. Continue evaluating Y on more distinct cases rather than treating complete coverage of this small fixture as approval.

For variant A, replace the baseline version line with refund-eval-1 | presentation-v1 | saved-verdicts-1 | revision repair. In X, the exact changed lines are X2: 90.00 (2 scored), attempted 7/8 | valid 6/7 | scorable 5/6 | end-to-end 5/8, micro mean 86.00 | median 90.00 | min 70 | max 100 | range 30, row population variance 104.00 | row population SD 10.20, macro run mean 86.67 | run-mean population SD 3.33, and gaps X1/Q4:SKIPPED, X2/Q3:ABSTAIN, X2/Q4:TIMEOUT. These six lines each have two leading spaces. Every other line stays as in the baseline. The below-mean 80 increases scored coverage. X remains blocked.

For variant B, replace the baseline version line with refund-eval-1 | presentation-v1 | saved-verdicts-1 | revision abstain. In Y, the exact changed lines are Y2: 82.67 (3 scored), attempted 8/8 | valid 8/8 | scorable 7/8 | end-to-end 7/8, micro mean 82.57 | median 82.00 | min 76 | max 90 | range 14, row population variance 22.53 | row population SD 4.75, macro run mean 82.58 | run-mean population SD 0.08, gaps Y2/Q4:ABSTAIN, and decision REVIEW. These seven lines each have two leading spaces. Every other line stays as in the baseline. The valid abstention changes the score mix and calls for review even though a policy failure was not observed.

Knowledge Check

  1. Two runs disagree on the same saved reply. What would you fix in the experiment to investigate judge variation?
  2. What does an 80% mean tell you about a series with scores 70%, 80%, and 90%?
  3. In the list 70, 80, 80, 80, 90, replace 90 with 20. Why does the median stay fixed?
  4. Two lists have the same minimum and maximum. What facts about their distribution could still differ?
  5. When would you divide by the number of values for variance, and what does the square root give you?
  6. One run has twice as many scored cases as another. How does the pooled mean weight the two runs?
  7. A judge output is a valid abstention. Which coverage counts include it and which score count excludes it?
  8. A setting consistently gives polished but wrong deadline advice. What should the engineering decision use?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Keep each captured reply, reference, rubric, effective judge configuration, and scoring rule fixed. Compare repeated judge verdicts by case rather than regenerating the reply.
  2. The observed center is 80%. The mean gives no count of distinct cases and no explanation for the low or high runs.
  3. Sorting yields 20, 70, 80, 80, 80. The middle position still holds 80. The mean changes because the sum changes.
  4. The values inside the extremes could be clustered in the middle or near the edges. Their means, medians, and standard deviations may differ.
  5. Divide by the full count to describe the population variance of the saved list. Its square root is population standard deviation, in the same units as the original scores.
  6. The run with twice as many scored cases contributes twice as many rows, so it receives twice the weight in the pooled mean. An equal-run mean gives each run half.
  7. Count the attempt and valid record. Leave it out of the scorable count and numeric mean. Report the abstention as its own status.
  8. Apply the independent policy rule and block the confirmed contradiction. Use the score series to understand presentation stability and collect more paired evidence after correcting the policy behavior.

Common Mistakes

When percentages move, open the run and case records first. Identify which settings applied, which answers were reused or generated anew, and which judge outputs were valid.

Repeated values on one question reveal what happened on that question. Keep the number of distinct questions separate.

Publish score coverage and the policy gate beside any average. Missing scores change the denominator, and a high presentation score can accompany a wrong policy claim.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Replay saved outcomes to reproduce the math. Use controlled repeats to investigate response or judge variability. Keep the analysis unit, variance convention, weights, and coverage clear. Inspect critical facts and missing evidence before drawing a release conclusion.

Next, Confidence intervals, significance and sample size asks how much uncertainty remains when you compare settings on paired cases.

    About the Course

    Vision and audience

    A long-term reference for learners entering LLM evaluation, engineers owning evaluation decisions, and instructors teaching or adapting practical labs. By the end of the core path, a learner should be able to design a versioned evaluation, build and calibrate scorers, quantify uncertainty, diagnose RAG and agent failures, and defend a production release decision. Expertise includes knowing when the evidence warrants another experiment or human review.

    Start with concepts and explicit decision criteria, then build a small Python scorer. Use frameworks once learners can explain the metric and verify a result by hand. Study RAG and agents through observable inputs, outputs and states. Finish by connecting offline evaluations to release decisions, traces and monitored outcomes. The plan describes target competencies and future labs. The coverage statuses describe the current repository.

    Sequence and time estimates

    Core progression spans Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced and Production. Specialized / Expert modules are electives that can be studied independently after their listed prerequisites. Topic records give the minimum preparation for focused study. The recommended module order provides a complete beginner route. Required study for an individual module is computed from the prerequisites of its topics. Each stage ends with a reviewable artifact, and the capstone brings those artifacts together.

    Times are planning estimates in hours. Each topic lists theory, guided hands-on implementation, independent experiments and interpretation, exercises and assessment, total learner time, and instructor-led classroom time. Instructor-led hours are a separate delivery estimate for explanation, demonstration and supervised practice. Preparation, breaks, and optional provider work are outside that estimate. Plan extra preparation for a first teaching run.

    Estimates assume a learner who can use a terminal and read simple Python, coaching available for the first lab, and prepared fixtures with expected outputs. Guided times include routine setup and troubleshooting for the activity. Learners new to Python should practice reading a JSON file, looping over records, and running a test before starting guided implementation. Large downloads, hardware delays, provider wait times, deep remediation and elective live extensions vary by environment. Pilot time estimates with both a beginner and an experienced engineer.

    One evolving application

    • Beginner — Evaluate a fictional bank support chatbot from six saved responses. Build exact/semantic boundary examples, a deterministic scorer and a blind human review sheet. Explain failure, uncertainty and execution error.
    • Intermediate — Publish a versioned gold dataset, calibrate a judge on frozen examples and compare prompt versions with paired Python analysis. Verify labels, denominators and uncertainty before drawing a conclusion.
    • Advanced RAG — Give the chatbot a fictional policy corpus. Evaluate ranked passages, context sufficiency, claims and citations, then compare retrieval changes against an oracle reference.
    • Advanced agents and safety — Add a mock account lookup and a simulated workflow. Verify actions, arguments, state, recovery and safe refusals. Assess defensive controls from fixed fictional traces and inert records.
    • Production — Add fixture-driven gates, trace metrics and a simulated incident. Convert a reviewed failure into a regression fixture and defend a release, hold or rollback decision.
    • Electives — Change the task when the method needs different evidence. Use synthetic fee charts for multimodal evaluation, public-style and private fictional benchmarks for contamination lessons, and benign generated functions for test-driven code evaluation. Use the healthcare examples for transfer lessons on score validity and source grounding.

    Execution modes and tool choices

    Every essential lesson starts with a fixture or simulated run that needs no model, network or credentials. Live Ollama inference and locally cached embeddings are optional hands-on extensions. The existing Test 5 configuration points to OpenAI and the existing Test 10 RAGAS integration requires OpenAI calls. These examples are references until local or fixture alternatives and effective settings are verified. Hosted graders and paid comparisons are optional, explicitly budgeted extensions.

    Choose DeepEval for Python-oriented assertions and thresholds when its chosen metric fits the construct. Choose RAGAS for a RAG metric suite when the record carries its required references or evidence. Both may call judges or embeddings and need versioned adapters, explicit failure states and checked denominator behavior. Choose promptfoo for a declarative prompt and provider matrix, and OpenAI Evals for an OpenAI-centered managed grading workflow when supported graders, data handling and cost fit. Compare both on saved cases before adding a managed run.

    Choose Langfuse for linked LLM traces, observations and scores. It depends on the quality of instrumented events and attached scores. OpenTelemetry is useful when correlation across services is the objective, with separate application quality measures. In defensive evaluation, Garak illustrates scanner-style coverage and PyRIT illustrates organized assessment records. Use prepared offline reports to compare their evidence formats and coverage. Tool output depends on scope, fixtures and labels, and requires review before it informs a decision.

    Instructor Resources

    Teaching Plan

    Mandatory lesson standard

    1. State observable learning objectives.
    2. Give prerequisites, setup, input artifacts and an entry checkpoint.
    3. Explain the concept in plain language.
    4. Explain why it exists.
    5. State the problem it solves and constraints on use.
    6. Give realistic engineering use cases.
    7. Work a small example by hand with a known answer.
    8. Increase complexity gradually, including a conflicting or ambiguous case.
    9. Give a step-by-step Python implementation or reproducible Python replay when the topic concerns a managed workflow.
    10. Explain code sections that change behavior, scores or denominators.
    11. Show expected artifacts and key execution results.
    12. Interpret results and what decisions they can support.
    13. Demonstrate common mistakes.
    14. Explain limitations and failure cases, including evaluator failure where relevant.
    15. Include a guided experiment with one controlled variable.
    16. Assign independent exercises with measurable outputs.
    17. Provide solutions or verification criteria, including accepted alternative solutions.
    18. Include instructor notes with timing, prediction prompts, common learner errors and offline fallback.
    19. Document troubleshooting and how to identify failure stage.
    20. Include knowledge checks and observable completion criteria.
    21. Connect the current topic to earlier and later evaluation decisions.

    Classroom preparation and assessment

    Each session should use the topic's prerequisite check and demonstrations, then ask learners to predict a result before running it. Prepare a small known-answer fixture, one common misconception and a harder case. Grade claims against evidence and review inclusion, decision policy and exceptions. Where output is stochastic, grade expected invariants and justified decisions. For the capstone, require an annotated dataset, manifest, replayable report, failure diagnosis and release recommendation. Ask a peer to reproduce the result.

    At least one teaching variant for core labs should use standard-library Python and prepared data. Where a framework is the objective, provide a fixture containing its inputs and results and prepare a pinned optional environment. Instructors should try the first run on target classroom hardware and define bounds for compute, data handling and spend before optional live sessions.

    Implementation sequence

    1. First milestone — Deliver the M01–M03 fixture-first slice, the starter M04-T01 schema and the first M06-T01 judge replay. Use exactly shared response IDs across the human, rule and judge evidence. Supply a handout, annotated answer key, instructor demonstration and local fixture verification before updating requirements for optional runs.
    2. Build the dataset and measurement spine in M04–M07. Establish reliable denominators, anchors, held-out cases, paired comparisons and uncertainty exercises before publishing example baselines.
    3. Add M08–M12 around the same contract. Reuse the banking corpus and traces. Verify gold passage and final-state controls before framework demos. Prepare safety and defensive-review fixtures for bounded, fictional labs.
    4. Add M13–M15 after the offline gates are stable. Introduce sampled synthetic traffic, redacted tracing and incident-to-regression review.
    5. Build electives once the relevant core artifacts are stable. Add tracks based on learner need and verify each against a separate domain-specific rubric.

    Maintenance, versioning and regeneration

    Curriculum revision 1.1.

    Use stable module and topic IDs. Edit titles and passages in place. Allocate new IDs for new learning objectives and preserve old IDs in a deprecation record when retiring a topic. Increment the curriculum revision when changing expected competencies, prerequisites or coverage. Version datasets, prompts, model snapshots and evaluator definitions independently and link those versions from lesson materials.

    Update the per-topic mapping whenever a lesson or experiment changes. Review all dependent topics when a prerequisite changes. A topic is ready for implementation sign-off when the lesson follows the standard, an instructor has replayed it, a learner can verify its output and the audit-linked corrections are resolved or documented. Re-estimate time after actual pilots, and record scope changes with the relevant IDs.

    The Markdown is authoritative. Run python3 docs/generate_master_curriculum.py from the repository root with Python 3.10 or newer to regenerate the standalone HTML. Use python3 docs/generate_master_curriculum.py --check to verify the checked-in artifact matches exactly. Edit the structured Markdown fields and rerun the generator. Use explicit anchors for IDs, comma-separated mandatory and recommended topic links, and the fixed time column order. Use a link followed by an em dash and a named exercise for each conditional prerequisite, with slash-separated entries when needed. Update the Paths A–G table when a target or required dependency changes. The generator validates finding IDs against the audit when that file is present. The HTML is a portable view of the plan. Repository lesson links require the companion lesson files. Progress is stored in the browser for the current device and may depend on file URL and privacy settings.
